modules.title: Cybersecurity foundations
modules.summary: Security keeps information and systems confidential, intact and available while someone is trying to make them otherwise, so every security test traces back to one of those properties.

objectives.text: Explain confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity and accountability with a failure and a first test idea for each.
Distinguish asset, threat, vulnerability, exploit and risk, and name the four risk treatments.
Explain least privilege, defence in depth, fail securely, complete mediation and zero trust.
Recall the shape of the Cyber Kill Chain and of MITRE ATT&CK (15 Enterprise tactics in v20).

keyPoints: Risk = likelihood x impact, judged per scenario, not per vulnerability.
AAA is authentication, authorization and accounting; most real findings are failures of authorization.
A security audit checks conformance; a security test checks resistance. They complement each other.
Know HTTP, cookies, headers, same-origin policy, TLS, DNS, hashing vs encryption vs signing, SSO and OAuth, Linux permissions and cloud IAM.
Learn ATT&CK tactics in order from the live matrix, not from old posters.
practice: Pick one feature of an app you know and write one failure and one first test per CIA property.
Intercept one login request in a proxy and label every header and cookie.

modules.title: ISTQB security testing core
modules.summary: ISTQB is replacing the 2016 CT-SEC syllabus with CT-STE (launched February 2025) and a planned CT-STA. Study the shared core and keep a crosswalk so your notes survive the transition.

objectives.text: Recall the CT-STE and CT-SEC exam formats and prerequisites.
Explain how protection level, policies and standards shape test depth and test oracles.
Map each CT-SEC chapter to its CT-STE counterpart.
Explain K1 to K4 and how to use exam time on scenario questions.

keyPoints: CT-STE: 40 questions, 43 points, 28 to pass (65%), 75 minutes, CTFL required. CT-SEC: 45 questions, 80 points, 52 to pass, 120 minutes, CTFL plus three years.
Non-native-language candidates get 25% more time; no grandfathering from CT-SEC to CT-STE or CT-STA.
CT-SEC has a human-factors chapter that CT-STE does not; CT-STE adds ISMS, context and standards chapters.
Standards supply test oracles, vocabulary and audit evidence; checklist-only testing gives false assurance.
CTFL treats security as a non-functional characteristic; CTAL-TTA section 4.3 has two K2 objectives.
practice: Read the official CT-STE syllabus PDF and tick each learning objective you can explain without notes.
Take ten flashcards from this topic daily until all are in box 4 or higher.

modules.title: Security test process and risk-based planning
modules.summary: A security test runs through plan, design, execute, evaluate and maintain; the first stage decides whether the rest are legal, safe and aimed at the risks that matter.

objectives.text: Explain the five stages with their outputs and common pitfalls.
Write scenarios as actor, goal, path and asset, rate them and assign test depth.
Apply equivalence partitioning, boundary values, decision tables and state transitions to security.
Choose entry and exit criteria and safety rails for execution.

keyPoints: Written authorisation, scope, windows and an emergency contact come before the first test.
Coverage is measured against threat-model elements, requirements, ASVS or Top 10 items and attack-surface items.
Use abuse cases, attack trees, error guessing, exploratory charters, combinatorial testing and fuzzing alongside classic techniques.
Test only in the approved environment, log every action, avoid destructive tests, keep no real personal data.
The test-case library (46 cases) gives ready-made positive, negative, boundary and exploratory cases.
practice: Write five scenarios for a web shop in actor-goal-path-asset form and rank them in a table.
Pick ten cases from the library, adapt them to a feature you know and run them in your lab.

modules.title: Security testing across the SDLC and DevSecOps
modules.summary: Security testing works best when every lifecycle stage has a control and a test that proves it works, so defects are caught where they are introduced.

objectives.text: Match a security activity and a verification to each lifecycle stage.
State what SAST, SCA, DAST, IAST, secret scanning and fuzzing find and miss.
Design pipeline gates that block only on high-confidence results and gate on changed code.
Describe SSDF, SAMM, BSIMM, SLSA and SBOM formats.

keyPoints: Scanner output is not the test: authorization and business-logic flaws need scripted and manual tests.
Secure the pipeline too: runners, tokens, third-party actions and build caches are targets.
Findings need an owner, a fix-by date and time-boxed exceptions.
Shift left and add shift-right controls: production monitoring, disclosure channel, bug bounty.
Track false-positive rate, time to fix and escapes to tune gates.
practice: Add Semgrep, a dependency scanner and a secret scanner to a public repository's CI.
Write one role-by-object test for an endpoint and add it to the regression suite.

modules.title: Web application security testing
modules.summary: Three OWASP documents do three jobs: the Top 10 raises awareness, ASVS lists requirements to verify and WSTG explains how to test. The CWE Top 25 adds a weakness-level view.

objectives.text: Recall OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 to A10 and the main changes from 2021.
Turn Top 10 categories and ASVS requirements into test ideas.
Relate WSTG categories 4.1 to 4.12 to the Top 10.
Run a practical web test sequence and the quick checks for cookies, headers, sessions, errors and files.

keyPoints: Access control is first; Security Misconfiguration moved to second; supply chain widened A03; SSRF merged into A01; A10 is new.
ASVS 5.0.0 (30 May 2025) has three levels; choose a level from risk.
CWE Top 25 2025 starts with XSS (79), SQL injection (89), CSRF (352), missing authorization (862) and out-of-bounds write (787).
Work through WSTG in risk order, starting with authorization and authentication; verify by hand; rate with CVSS; tag with CWE.
Quick checks: cookie flags, security headers, new session ID at login, no stack traces, server-side upload checks.
practice: Solve Juice Shop or Web Security Academy labs on access control, authentication, injection and XSS.
Write a one-page finding for one lab in the report format from the pen-testing module.

modules.title: API security testing
modules.summary: APIs expose business logic directly, so the most serious API defects are authorization failures that a user interface would have hidden.

objectives.text: Recall the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023).
Build a role x endpoint x object matrix and automate it.
Describe protocol-specific checks for REST, GraphQL, JWT, OAuth 2.0 and webhooks.
Test limits and sensitive business flows within an agreed budget.

keyPoints: API1 is object-level authorization; hard-to-guess IDs are not a control.
Compare the specification with observed traffic to find undocumented endpoints.
Schemathesis and RESTler generate negative and boundary tests from a specification.
GraphQL: depth and complexity limits, batching and aliasing, field-level authorization, no introspection in production.
Report with API Top 10 ID, CWE and CVSS, and add the failing request to the regression suite.
practice: Run OWASP crAPI locally and find one BOLA and one BFLA issue.
Write a script that replays each endpoint as two users and flags differences.

modules.title: Testing security mechanisms
modules.summary: A security mechanism counts only if a test shows it works. ISTQB asks testers to check the effectiveness of hardening, access control, encryption, network controls, detection, malware scanning, obfuscation and training.

objectives.text: Plan an effectiveness test for each mechanism.
Apply SP 800-63B-4 as an oracle for passwords, sessions and recovery.
Recognise cryptography misuse patterns.
Test network boundaries, egress and the detection chain end to end.

keyPoints: Passwords: 15 characters minimum for single factor, 8 with MFA, 64 or more accepted, no composition rules, breach blocklist.
Sessions: new ID after login, server-side invalidation, idle and absolute timeouts, cookie flags.
TLS 1.2 or later, 1.3 preferred; Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt for passwords; authenticated encryption; keys outside code.
Horizontal and vertical authorization tests; test every cell of the matrix and the indirect paths.
A detection rule that fires into an unread inbox is a failed control.
practice: Write boundary tests for a password field using 7, 8, 14, 15, 64 and 65 characters.
Scan a lab server's TLS configuration and explain each finding.

modules.title: Mobile, cloud, containers and infrastructure
modules.summary: Outside the browser the same questions apply, who can reach what and what happens when a control fails, but the attack surface changes.

objectives.text: Name the reference and first tests for mobile, cloud, containers, IaC, networks and OT.
Outline a mobile, cloud or container test.
Use the shared responsibility model to place findings.

keyPoints: MASVS has eight control groups; MASTG is the testing guide.
Cloud: read the provider's testing policy, start with identity, look for public storage and metadata exposure.
Containers: scan images, run non-root, no privileged mode, review RBAC and admission control.
IaC: scan in the pull request and compare deployed state with code to find drift.
OT: passive observation and agreed windows; active scans can stop equipment.
practice: Scan a small Terraform or Kubernetes manifest with Checkov or Trivy and fix two findings.
Open an Android or iOS practice app from the OWASP MAS project and inspect its local storage.

modules.title: AI and LLM security testing
modules.summary: Text is both data and instruction, so anyone who controls text the model reads may steer what it does. Test the whole system, not only the model.

objectives.text: Recall the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025).
Build an evaluation harness with repeated attack prompts and a success rate.
Relate ATLAS, ATT&CK v20, AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act to testing.

keyPoints: LLM01 prompt injection and LLM06 excessive agency combine in most agent incidents.
Run each attack many times; report a success rate; keep a regression suite across versions.
Test the non-model parts normally: authentication, authorization, rate limits, logging, secrets.
No secrets in prompts; enforce rules outside the prompt; encode model output.
Dates for EU AI Act high-risk obligations moved under the Digital Omnibus: verify the final text.
practice: Play a prompt-injection game, then write five regression prompts for a chatbot you control.
Run garak or promptfoo against a local model and record a success rate.

modules.title: Human factors and social engineering
modules.summary: Attackers often go after people because persuading a person is cheaper than defeating a technical control, so a complete test plan covers awareness and behaviour, ethically and with approval.

objectives.text: Explain how attackers think and which persuasion levers they use.
Match each social-engineering technique to its controls and ethical test approach.
Measure whether training works using behaviour metrics.

keyPoints: Phishing, vishing, smishing, baiting, tailgating, business email compromise, MFA fatigue and deepfakes each have a control and a test.
Report rate and time to report matter more than click rate.
Get written approval, report in aggregate, never name and shame, avoid lures that exploit distress, set stop conditions, debrief.
Insider risk: least privilege, separation of duties, logging, data-loss prevention, leaver process.
practice: Draft the approval and stop conditions for an imaginary phishing simulation.
Run a tabletop on a business-email-compromise scenario with two colleagues.

modules.title: Penetration testing, red teaming and vulnerability scoring
modules.summary: A penetration test is an authorised, time-boxed attempt to exploit weaknesses inside a defined scope and show real impact. Scoping and authorisation come first; scoring and reporting come last.

objectives.text: Distinguish assessment types and the questions they answer.
Describe NIST SP 800-115, PTES and OSSTMM phases.
Score and prioritise with CVE, CWE, CVSS v4.0, EPSS and KEV.
Write a report and run a disclosure process.

keyPoints: Pre-engagement: scope, rules of engagement, authorisation letter, windows, contacts, data handling, third-party permissions.
Use the minimum needed to prove impact; never bulk-copy real sensitive data; clean up; retest.
CVSS v4.0: Base, Threat, Environmental, Supplemental; bands none, low 0.1-3.9, medium 4.0-6.9, high 7.0-8.9, critical 9.0-10.0.
Prioritise by severity, likelihood (EPSS), observed exploitation (KEV), asset criticality and exposure.
Disclosure: security.txt, coordinated disclosure, ISO/IEC 29147 and 30111; CRA reporting from 11 September 2026.
practice: Write a full report for one Juice Shop finding using the bug-report template.
Score the same finding with CVSS v4.0 and explain each metric.

modules.title: Blue team: detection, incident response and vulnerability management
modules.summary: Blue-team work turns 'could this be attacked?' into 'would we notice, and could we recover?'. Logging, detection, response and recovery are controls too, so they need tests.

objectives.text: Test each link of the detection chain.
Describe the incident-response lifecycle and its CSF 2.0 reading.
Run the vulnerability management cycle with risk-based fix-by times.
Explain 3-2-1 backups, RPO and RTO and why restore drills matter.

keyPoints: Detection chain: telemetry, collection and integrity, rules, triage and response, tooling health.
Logging hygiene: no secrets, neutralise input, correlation IDs, separate security logs.
Incident response: prepare, practise, act, learn; blameless review with 5 Whys.
Vulnerability management: inventory, assess, prioritise, remediate, verify, report.
Metrics: time to detect and contain, ATT&CK coverage, false-positive rate, fix-by compliance, restore success.
practice: Install Wazuh or Security Onion in a lab and trigger a harmless Atomic Red Team test.
Write one Sigma rule and one test that proves it fires.

modules.title: Governance, risk, compliance and EU rules
modules.summary: Frameworks and laws tell you what an organisation must or should do about security; testers use them as test oracles, scope drivers and sources of evidence requirements.

objectives.text: Describe NIST CSF 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001, CIS Controls, SOC 2 and PCI DSS in one sentence each.
State the main testing and reporting hooks in GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act.
Trace tests to controls and keep evidence for audit.

keyPoints: Compliance is the floor: conformance is not resistance.
CRA reporting from 11 September 2026: 24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification, final report 14 days after a fix.
NIS2 steps are 24 hours, 72 hours and one month; GDPR breach notification is 72 hours; DORA requires threat-led testing at least every three years for designated entities.
A finding is a risk statement: feed it to the risk register with owner, treatment, date and residual risk.
Check national rules; dates and article numbers change as laws are amended.
practice: Map five library test cases to ISO/IEC 27001 or CSF 2.0 controls.
List what evidence an auditor would ask for after a penetration test.

modules.title: Security tools and labs
modules.summary: Tools find what they were built to find, so choose them by the job and the evidence you need. Skill comes from practice in places where breaking things is allowed.

objectives.text: Classify tools by purpose, white/grey/black-box and static/dynamic.
Select a tool from documented needs and avoid the common rollout traps.
Set up an isolated home lab and follow lab safety rules.

keyPoints: Selection: needs, fit, quality of results on your own code, open-source risks, vendor capabilities, cost and skills.
Traps: all rules on at once, unauthenticated scans, disruptive scans, tool as supply-chain target, output treated as verdict.
Labs: PortSwigger Web Security Academy, Juice Shop, crAPI, WebGoat, DVWA, OverTheWire, picoCTF, TryHackMe, Hack The Box and more.
Bind labs to localhost, snapshot before experiments, treat downloaded VMs as untrusted, never aim lab techniques at systems you do not own.
practice: Stand up Juice Shop with Docker bound to 127.0.0.1 and proxy it through ZAP or Burp.
Compare two tools for the same job on your own code and note false positives.

The CISA catalogue of vulnerabilities with observed exploitation.

Meeting a required standard. It is the floor: it shows conformance, not resistance.
Only authorised parties can read the information.
The deployed state diverging from its infrastructure-as-code definition.
Re-running a test to check that a fix worked.
Checking images for known vulnerabilities and unwanted contents.
Limiting the spread and impact of an incident.

An identifier for one specific, publicly disclosed vulnerability.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System; v4.0 has Base, Threat, Environmental and Supplemental metric groups.

Yearly ranking of the most dangerous software weaknesses; the 2025 list puts cross-site scripting (CWE-79) first.
Lockheed Martin model of seven linear attack stages, from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.

Tampering with training, fine-tuning or embedding data (LLM04).
Hiding real values by masking, tokenisation or anonymisation so those who should not see them cannot recover them.
Covering combinations of conditions; in security, every role x action x object cell of the access-control matrix.
Synthetic voice or video used to impersonate a trusted person.

Tricking a build into fetching a malicious public package instead of the internal package of the same name.
Building security checks and ownership into the development and operations pipeline.

EU Regulation 2022/2554 on digital operational resilience for financial entities, applying from 17 January 2025.
Running the system and observing its behaviour.
Endpoint detection and response: telemetry and response actions on endpoints.
Controlling outbound traffic, which limits how stolen data can leave.
A harmless standard file that antivirus products detect, used to test malware scanning.
Reversible protection with a key; symmetric uses one key, asymmetric a key pair.
Conditions that must hold before testing can start.
Exploit Prediction Scoring System: the probability that a vulnerability is exploited within 30 days.
Splitting inputs into classes that should behave alike; in security, valid, malformed and hostile classes.
Removing the cause of an incident from the environment.
Choosing tests from known weakness lists and experience, such as the OWASP Top 10.
Risk-based regulation of AI systems; the Digital Omnibus postpones the high-risk dates.
Cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements; vulnerability reporting starts 11 September 2026.
Curated attack prompts, automated runners and assertions on outputs and actions, kept as a regression suite.
Logs, requests and responses, and screenshots that support a finding; sanitise them and store them securely.
The model or agent has more tools, permissions or autonomy than it needs (LLM06).
Conditions that must hold before testing can stop.
A way of using a vulnerability.
A tool such as Metasploit for validating exploitability; authorised use only.
Time-boxed, charter-driven testing in which learning and test design happen together.
On error the system denies access (fails closed) instead of granting it.
A real weakness that testing failed to report.
A reported finding that is not a real weakness.
Feeding malformed or semi-valid inputs at scale to find crashes and unhandled cases.
EU data-protection regulation; Article 32 expects security appropriate to risk, Article 33 sets 72-hour breach notification.
A query feature that lists the schema; verbose in production it helps attackers map the API.
Testing with partial internal knowledge, such as test accounts and API documentation.
Reducing the attack surface by removing services, setting secure defaults and patching, compared with a baseline such as a CIS Benchmark.
One-way fingerprinting of data; for passwords use a slow, salted algorithm.
An isolated environment with an attacker machine and deliberately vulnerable targets.
Strict-Transport-Security: a response header telling browsers to use HTTPS only for the site.
Checking infrastructure-as-code templates for misconfigurations before deployment.
Identity and access management: cloud identities, roles and permissions.
Interactive application security testing: an agent inside the running application reports findings with code locations.
Insecure direct object reference: reaching another user's object by changing an identifier; in API terms BOLA.
Intrusion detection systems raise alerts; intrusion prevention systems also block.

Defining infrastructure in version-controlled templates, which can be scanned before deployment.

Unsafe handling of serialized data that lets an attacker alter program behaviour.
Risk from people with legitimate access, whether malicious or careless.
A cloud endpoint that hands credentials and data to workloads; exposure can allow token theft.
Information and systems cannot change without authorisation or without detection.

ISTQB cognitive level of a learning objective: K1 remember, K2 understand, K3 apply, K4 analyse.
Role-based access control for cluster resources.
Each account gets only the access its job needs.
Control characters in input that forge or corrupt log entries; neutralise user input before logging.

Repeated push prompts until someone approves one.
Knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on ATT&CK.
Knowledge base of adversary tactics, techniques and sub-techniques seen in real incidents; Enterprise v20 has 15 tactics.
Mean time to detect and mean time to contain.
Dividing a network into zones with controlled flows between them, default deny.
EU Directive 2022/2555 for essential and important entities, with 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month incident reporting steps.
Voluntary framework published in February 2024 with six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
Technical guide to security testing; its penetration-test phases are planning, discovery, attack and reporting.
Catalogue of security and privacy controls, including penetration testing and vulnerability scanning.
Authentication guideline, final 31 July 2025: 15-character minimum for single-factor passwords, no composition rules, breached-password check.
An actor cannot credibly deny having performed an action.
The US National Vulnerability Database, which enriches CVE records.
Authorization framework for delegated access; current guidance is the Security Best Current Practice, RFC 9700.
A machine-readable description of a REST API, compared with real traffic to find undocumented endpoints.
An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 used for single sign-on.
Systems that control physical processes; prefer passive observation when testing them.
ISECOM's metrics-driven methodology across human, physical, wireless, telecommunications and data-network channels.
Software Assurance Maturity Model, scored across five business functions: governance, design, implementation, verification, operations.
Awareness list of the ten biggest web application risk categories; the 2025 edition runs A01 to A10.
An open-source intercepting proxy and web scanner (Zed Attack Proxy) whose automation framework can run in a CI pipeline.
Using sequences such as ../ to reach files outside the intended directory.
Payment card data security standard; requirement 11 covers regular scans and penetration tests.
An authorised, time-boxed attempt to exploit weaknesses inside a defined scope and show real impact.
Authority, urgency, scarcity, social proof, reciprocity, liking and commitment.
Deceptive messages that push a click or a credential entry.
An authenticator bound to the real site so a lookalike cannot capture it; SP 800-63B-4 requires one at AAL3.
An automated check that can stop a build or release.
Proof Key for Code Exchange: protects the OAuth authorization-code flow for public clients.
The Kubernetes admission controller that enforces Pod Security Standards levels.
Deployment and security rules written as code and enforced automatically, for example with Open Policy Agent or Kyverno.
A tool such as Nmap that discovers open ports and services.
Activity after initial access; use the minimum needed to prove impact.
Inventing a believable scenario to obtain information or access.
Instructions hidden in text the model reads, directly or indirectly, steer it against policy (LLM01).
Penetration Testing Execution Standard: pre-engagement through reporting in seven phases.
A collaborative exercise in which attackers and defenders share each step.
The outcome depends on the timing of concurrent requests, for example a voucher used twice.
Capping how often a user, key or source may call a function.
A goal-based, often covert exercise that tests detection and response as well as prevention.
Checking that a change did not break or reopen something that worked.
The risk that remains after a treatment has been applied.
The chance and cost of a specific scenario; in its simplest form likelihood multiplied by impact, judged per scenario.
A list of risks, each with an owner, a treatment, a target date and the residual risk.
The choice to mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept a risk.
Directing test effort by the likelihood and impact of risks.
Recovery point objective is the most data you can lose; recovery time objective is the longest downtime you can accept.
The agreed rules for a test: scope, allowed techniques, windows, rate limits, contacts and data handling.
A unique random value added before hashing so identical passwords do not hash identically.
The browser rule restricting how documents and scripts from one origin interact with another.
XML-based single sign-on standard; validate signature, issuer, audience and expiry.
Static application security testing: analyses source code or bytecode without running it.
Software bill of materials: a list of the components inside software; formats include SPDX and CycloneDX.
Software composition analysis: finds known vulnerable versions and licence issues in third-party components.
Searching repositories and their history for keys and tokens committed by mistake.
The safe setting is the one you get without configuring anything.
A check of conformance to a policy or standard.
Relying on the secrecy of a design for protection. Assume the design is known and keep only keys and secrets secret.
An attempt to show whether controls withstand an attack scenario.
A standard file (RFC 9116) giving security contact details.
A pattern-based static-analysis tool whose rules look like the code they find; suited to fast checks in pull requests.
No single person can complete a sensitive action alone.
The attacker sets a known session ID before login; the defence is to issue a new ID at login.
The split of security duties between cloud provider and customer, used to place each finding.
Moving security activities earlier in the lifecycle, so defects are caught where they are introduced.
Adding production-side controls such as monitoring, a disclosure channel and bug bounty.
Security information and event management: collects and correlates logs and raises alerts.
A shared, vendor-neutral format for detection rules, mapped to ATT&CK techniques.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: levels for build integrity and provenance.
Phishing by SMS text message.
AICPA attestation against the trust services criteria.
Manipulating people into disclosing information or performing actions.
Everything that goes into building and delivering software: dependencies, build systems, signing and distribution.
Phishing tailored to a specific person or group.
Injection into database queries; prevented with parameterised queries.
NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SP 800-218): Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, Respond to Vulnerabilities.
Server-side request forgery: the server fetches a URL the attacker controls. In OWASP Top 10:2025 it sits inside A01.
Testing allowed and forbidden transitions; in security, replayed or out-of-order steps.
Inspecting code, configuration or design without running the system.
Threat categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege.
Extraction of hidden instructions, which should never hold secrets (LLM07).
A discussion-based rehearsal of an incident scenario.
Following an authorised person through a controlled door.
Records from endpoints, identity, network, cloud control plane, applications and email.
The information tests are derived from, such as requirements, policies, standards and threat models.
A source of the expected result, that is, what 'correct' means for a test.
A potential cause of harm, described by actor, capability and intent.
Structured analysis of what can go wrong in a design, using methods such as STRIDE, PASTA or LINDDUN.
The EU framework for threat-intelligence-based red-team testing in finance.
Transport Layer Security protects data in transit; use 1.2 or later, with 1.3 preferred.
An open-source scanner for container images, file systems and infrastructure-as-code that reports vulnerable packages, misconfigurations and secrets.
Excessive resource or cost use through long inputs, runaway loops or missing caps (LLM10).
Access-control and isolation flaws in retrieval stores (LLM08).
Voice phishing by phone, including help-desk impersonation.
A weakness that a threat can use.
Broad, mostly automated identification of weaknesses and their severity.
Tells researchers how to report a vulnerability safely.
The cycle of inventory, assess, prioritise, remediate or mitigate, verify and report.
An automated tool that checks systems for known weaknesses.
A callback request from one system to another; verify signatures and prevent replay with timestamps or nonces.
Testing with full knowledge of the internals, such as source code.
A packet analyser that shows network traffic frame by frame; used to inspect protocols and TLS handshakes.
Signed permission from someone entitled to give it, naming the tester, targets and dates. No test runs without it.
OWASP Web Security Testing Guide: explains how to test, in categories 4.1 to 4.12 on the latest branch.
Never grant access because of network location; verify identity, device and context for each request (NIST SP 800-207).

flashcards.q: What does the CIA triad stand for?
flashcards.a: Confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three core properties every security test traces back to.

flashcards.q: What is risk in its simplest form?
flashcards.a: Likelihood multiplied by impact, judged per scenario rather than per vulnerability.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a threat and a vulnerability?
flashcards.a: A threat is a potential cause of harm (actor, capability, intent). A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use.

flashcards.q: Name the four risk-treatment options.
flashcards.a: Mitigate, transfer, avoid or accept. What remains afterwards is residual risk.

flashcards.q: What does AAA stand for?
flashcards.a: Authentication (who are you), authorization (what may you do) and accounting (what did you do).

flashcards.q: What is the attack surface?
flashcards.a: The sum of entry points an attacker can reach: endpoints, ports, forms, files, integrations and staff.

flashcards.q: What is defence in depth?
flashcards.a: Several independent layers of control, so one failure is not a breach.

flashcards.q: What do least privilege and separation of duties require?
flashcards.a: Each account gets only what its job needs, and no single person can complete a sensitive action alone.

flashcards.q: What does 'fail securely' mean?
flashcards.a: On error the system denies access instead of granting it (fails closed), and the safe setting is the default.

flashcards.q: What is complete mediation?
flashcards.a: Every access is checked every time, on the server.

flashcards.q: What does zero trust say about network location?
flashcards.a: Never grant access because of where a request comes from; verify identity, device and context per request (NIST SP 800-207).

flashcards.q: How does a security audit differ from a security test?
flashcards.a: An audit checks conformance to a policy or standard; a test tries to show whether controls resist an attack scenario. They complement each other.

flashcards.q: Which six sub-characteristics does ISO/IEC 25010:2023 list under security?
flashcards.a: Confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity and resistance.

flashcards.q: How many tactics does MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise have in v20, and what changed in v19?
flashcards.a: 15 tactics. Version 19 split Defense Evasion into Stealth and Defense Impairment.

flashcards.q: How many stages has the Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain?
flashcards.a: Seven linear stages, from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.

flashcards.q: Which algorithms are recommended for password storage?
flashcards.a: Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, with unique salts.

flashcards.q: Which ISTQB certificates succeed the single 2016 CT-SEC syllabus?
flashcards.a: CT-STE (Security Test Engineer, launched February 2025) and a planned CT-STA (Security Test Analyst, scheduled for 2026 but unconfirmed in October 2026).

flashcards.q: What are the CT-STE exam numbers?
flashcards.a: 40 questions, 43 points, 28 points to pass (65%), 75 minutes.

flashcards.q: What are the CT-SEC exam numbers?
flashcards.a: 45 questions, 80 points, 52 points to pass (65%), 120 minutes.

flashcards.q: What do K1, K2, K3 and K4 stand for?
flashcards.a: K1 remember, K2 understand, K3 apply, K4 analyse.

flashcards.q: What is the prerequisite for CT-STE?
flashcards.a: The ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL).

flashcards.q: What is the prerequisite for CT-SEC?
flashcards.a: CTFL plus three years of relevant experience.

flashcards.q: How much extra exam time do non-native-language candidates get?
flashcards.a: 25% more.

flashcards.q: At which K-level are keywords and security domain terms examinable in CT-STE?
flashcards.a: K1 (remember).

flashcards.q: Which CT-SEC theme has no dedicated CT-STE chapter?
flashcards.a: Human factors in security testing (CT-SEC chapter 6).

flashcards.q: Which CT-STE chapter covers the security test process?
flashcards.a: Chapter 3, The Security Test Process (120 minutes).

flashcards.q: What are the five stages of the security test process in the 2016 syllabus?
flashcards.a: Planning, design, execution, evaluation and maintenance.

flashcards.q: Does ISTQB grandfather CT-SEC holders into CT-STE or CT-STA?
flashcards.a: No. ISTQB states that no grandfathering applies; holders must pass the new exam to hold those titles.

flashcards.q: Which CTAL-TTA section covers security testing?
flashcards.a: Section 4.3 Security Testing, with two K2 objectives and no objective on techniques or tools.

flashcards.q: How does CTFL v4.0.1 treat security?
flashcards.a: As one of the non-functional quality characteristics that testers evaluate.

flashcards.q: What do standards give a security tester?
flashcards.a: Test oracles (what 'correct' means), a shared vocabulary and audit evidence.

flashcards.q: What should test depth follow, according to ISTQB's security paradigms?
flashcards.a: Asset value and information sensitivity: protection level follows them, so test effort should too.

flashcards.q: What does the hub read into CT-STE section 8.3 about hiding versus avoiding a weakness?
flashcards.a: Hiding puts a barrier in front of a weakness (a filter) and buys time; avoiding changes design or code so the weakness no longer exists. This is the hub's reading; confirm it in the syllabus.

flashcards.q: Name the five stages of the security test process.
flashcards.a: Plan, design, execute, evaluate, maintain.

flashcards.q: What must exist before the first security test runs?
flashcards.a: Written authorisation from someone entitled to give it, with scope, time windows and an emergency contact (rules of engagement).

flashcards.q: What is risk-based security testing?
flashcards.a: Spending test effort where likelihood and impact are highest: rank scenarios, then assign test depth, techniques and tools.

flashcards.q: How do you write a security scenario?
flashcards.a: As actor, goal, path and asset, for example a customer reads another customer's invoice by changing an ID.

flashcards.q: Give example entry criteria for a security test.
flashcards.a: Signed authorisation, scope list, representative non-production data, one test account per role, an identified build and a baseline scan.

flashcards.q: Give example exit criteria for a security test.
flashcards.a: Every high-priority scenario executed; no open critical or high finding without documented risk acceptance; fixes retested; report reviewed by the system owner.

flashcards.q: What is security coverage measured against?
flashcards.a: Something concrete: threat-model elements, security requirements and abuse cases, ASVS or Top 10 items, attack-surface items; for white-box work, code paths and CWE classes.

flashcards.q: How do you apply boundary value analysis to security?
flashcards.a: Probe limits of length, size, rate and time: lockout at N and N+1 failures, upload limit plus one byte, token expiry plus or minus one second.

flashcards.q: How do you apply state transition testing to security?
flashcards.a: Attack out-of-order or replayed steps: reuse a reset link after the password changed, skip a checkout step, reuse an old session.

flashcards.q: How do you apply decision tables to access control?
flashcards.a: Cover every role x action x object cell of the access-control matrix with an allowed and a denied case.

flashcards.q: What is an abuse case?
flashcards.a: A use case mirrored from the attacker's side, for example 'As an attacker I reuse a one-time link'.

flashcards.q: What is an attack tree?
flashcards.a: A decomposition of an attacker's goal into sub-goals. Root 'take over account' with leaves such as credential stuffing, reset-flow flaw and session theft.

flashcards.q: Name safety rails for executing security tests.
flashcards.a: Approved environment and window; stop condition and emergency contact; dedicated accounts and snapshots; throttled, non-destructive tests; every action logged; evidence stored securely.

flashcards.q: Why is 'one happy path plus one stock payload per field' weak test design?
flashcards.a: It misses authorization, state, logic and boundary failures. Security tests should state the secure expected behaviour for each risk.

flashcards.q: What is the common pitfall in the Plan stage?
flashcards.a: Testing production by default or without written permission.

flashcards.q: What is the common pitfall in the Evaluate stage?
flashcards.a: Severity inflated or played down without a rationale.

flashcards.q: What is shift-left security testing?
flashcards.a: Moving security checks earlier (requirements, design, code, CI) so defects are caught where they are introduced; pair it with shift-right controls such as monitoring.

flashcards.q: What does SAST analyse, and what does it miss?
flashcards.a: Source code or bytecode. It finds injection patterns, hard-coded secrets and unsafe APIs early, but misses business-logic flaws and runtime configuration and gives many false positives.

flashcards.q: What does SCA find and not find?
flashcards.a: Known vulnerable versions and licence issues in third-party components. It cannot find unknown flaws or tell you whether the vulnerable code is reachable.

flashcards.q: What does DAST test, and where does it struggle?
flashcards.a: The running application from outside: misconfiguration, missing headers, reflected injection, exposed endpoints. It struggles with deep authenticated flows and authorization or logic flaws.

flashcards.q: What is IAST?
flashcards.a: Interactive testing with an agent inside the running application, giving precise findings with code location during functional tests; it needs instrumentation.

flashcards.q: What is an SBOM, and which two formats are common?
flashcards.a: A list of the components inside software. SPDX (ISO/IEC 5962:2021) and CycloneDX (ECMA-424).

flashcards.q: What is SLSA?
flashcards.a: Levels for the build integrity and provenance of software artifacts.

flashcards.q: What are the four SSDF practice groups?
flashcards.a: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, Respond to Vulnerabilities.

flashcards.q: What is OWASP SAMM?
flashcards.a: A maturity model scored across five business functions: governance, design, implementation, verification and operations.

flashcards.q: How does BSIMM differ from SAMM?
flashcards.a: BSIMM is observational: it describes what real organisations do (governance, intelligence, SSDL touchpoints, deployment). SAMM is a model you score yourself against.

flashcards.q: How do teams keep pipeline gates from being switched off?
flashcards.a: Gate on new findings in changed code, not the whole backlog, and block only on high-confidence, high-severity results.

flashcards.q: Give three results that should block a pipeline.
flashcards.a: A detected secret, a critical vulnerability with an available fix, an unsigned artifact. Warn on the rest.

flashcards.q: Which three threat-modelling methods does the hub name?
flashcards.a: STRIDE, PASTA and LINDDUN (for privacy).

flashcards.q: What does the OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks list treat as an attack target?
flashcards.a: The pipeline itself: runners, tokens, third-party actions and build caches.

flashcards.q: Name two DevSecOps failure modes.
flashcards.a: Treating scanner output as the test; securing the application but not the pipeline; findings with no owner; exceptions that never expire; shift-left only.

flashcards.q: What is policy as code?
flashcards.a: Release rules written as code and enforced by admission and policy checks, for example with Open Policy Agent or Kyverno.

flashcards.q: List OWASP Top 10:2025 A01 to A10.
flashcards.a: A01 Broken Access Control; A02 Security Misconfiguration; A03 Software Supply Chain Failures; A04 Cryptographic Failures; A05 Injection; A06 Insecure Design; A07 Authentication Failures; A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures; A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures; A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

flashcards.q: What are the different jobs of the Top 10, ASVS and WSTG?
flashcards.a: Top 10 raises awareness of the biggest risk categories; ASVS lists requirements to verify; WSTG explains how to test.

flashcards.q: What changed from the 2021 Top 10 to 2025?
flashcards.a: Security Misconfiguration rose from 5th to 2nd, Cryptographic Failures fell 2nd to 4th, Injection 3rd to 5th, Insecure Design 4th to 6th; supply chain widened 'vulnerable components'; SSRF merged into Broken Access Control; A10 is new.

flashcards.q: What data underlies the 2025 Top 10?
flashcards.a: More than 2.8 million applications across 589 CWEs, plus a practitioner survey for risks that automated data under-represents.

flashcards.q: When was ASVS 5.0.0 published and how many levels does it define?
flashcards.a: 30 May 2025; three verification levels. Version 5.0 made Level 1 easier to reach and expanded Level 3 to roughly 90 requirements.

flashcards.q: Which weakness tops the 2025 CWE Top 25, and which follow?
flashcards.a: CWE-79 cross-site scripting, then CWE-89 SQL injection, CWE-352 CSRF, CWE-862 missing authorization and CWE-787 out-of-bounds write.

flashcards.q: Which WSTG category covers authorization testing?
flashcards.a: 4.5 Authorization Testing (ATHZ): path traversal, privilege escalation, insecure object references.

flashcards.q: Which WSTG category covers business logic and file upload?
flashcards.a: 4.10 Business Logic Testing (BUSL).

flashcards.q: Which flags should a session cookie carry?
flashcards.a: Secure, HttpOnly and a suitable SameSite value.

flashcards.q: Which response headers are quick checks?
flashcards.a: Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy and cache controls on sensitive pages.

flashcards.q: How do you prevent SQL injection?
flashcards.a: Parameterised queries, with validation as defence in depth and least-privilege database accounts.

flashcards.q: How do you prevent cross-site scripting?
flashcards.a: Context-aware output encoding, plus validation and a Content-Security-Policy as further layers.

flashcards.q: Where does SSRF sit in the 2025 Top 10?
flashcards.a: Inside A01 Broken Access Control.

flashcards.q: What does A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions cover?
flashcards.a: Poor error handling, logic errors and failing open. Test by forcing timeouts, malformed input and dependency failures and confirm the system fails closed without leaking details.

flashcards.q: How should uploaded files be handled?
flashcards.a: Type-checked on the server by content, not only name; stored outside the web root; never executed.

flashcards.q: What does A03 Software Supply Chain Failures cover?
flashcards.a: Compromised or vulnerable dependencies, build systems and distribution paths.

flashcards.q: What is API1:2023?
flashcards.a: Broken Object Level Authorization: a user reaches other users' objects by changing an identifier. Hard-to-guess IDs are not a control.

flashcards.q: What is API3:2023?
flashcards.a: Broken Object Property Level Authorization: responses expose too many fields, or writes accept fields the user must not set (mass assignment).

flashcards.q: What is API5:2023?
flashcards.a: Broken Function Level Authorization: ordinary users reach administrative functions by changing the method or path.

flashcards.q: What is API6:2023?
flashcards.a: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows: automation abuses a legitimate flow at scale, such as vouchers or sign-ups.

flashcards.q: List the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) names.
flashcards.a: API1 BOLA, API2 Broken Authentication, API3 BOPLA, API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption, API5 BFLA, API6 Sensitive Business Flows, API7 SSRF, API8 Security Misconfiguration, API9 Improper Inventory Management, API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs.

flashcards.q: What is API10:2023?
flashcards.a: Unsafe Consumption of APIs: the API trusts data from third-party services. Treat upstream data as untrusted.

flashcards.q: How do you test for BOLA?
flashcards.a: With two accounts, request each object type, including list, search, export and batch endpoints, using the other account's IDs.

flashcards.q: How do you get systematic coverage of API authorization?
flashcards.a: Build a role x endpoint x object matrix (a decision table) and automate it with scripts or a proxy extension such as Autorize.

flashcards.q: Which tools generate negative and boundary API tests from a specification?
flashcards.a: Schemathesis (property-based) and RESTler (stateful fuzzing).

flashcards.q: Which GraphQL issues should you check?
flashcards.a: Introspection and verbose errors in production, query depth and complexity limits, batching and aliasing used to dodge rate limits, and field-level authorization.

flashcards.q: What should you check on JWTs and OAuth 2.0?
flashcards.a: Signature validation and an algorithm allow-list; issuer, audience and expiry; short access tokens and refresh rotation; PKCE for public clients; exact redirect-URI matching; least-privilege scopes.

flashcards.q: How do you secure webhooks?
flashcards.a: Verify signatures and prevent replay with timestamps or nonces.

flashcards.q: Which version of the API Top 10 is current in October 2026?
flashcards.a: The 2023 edition; the OWASP site lists only 2023 and 2019.

flashcards.q: What password length rules does NIST SP 800-63B-4 set?
flashcards.a: At least 15 characters when the password is the only factor, 8 when it is one factor among several, and support for at least 64 characters.

flashcards.q: What else does SP 800-63B-4 say about passwords?
flashcards.a: No composition rules, no forced periodic changes, a blocklist check against compromised passwords, and password managers and paste must work.

flashcards.q: Which password lengths do you test at the boundaries?
flashcards.a: 7, 8, 14, 15, 64 and 65 characters, plus spaces and Unicode, a known breached password and paste.

flashcards.q: What should happen to a session at login and logout?
flashcards.a: A new unpredictable ID at login and privilege change; server-side invalidation at logout and password change; idle and absolute timeouts.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between horizontal and vertical authorization tests?
flashcards.a: Horizontal: the same role on someone else's data. Vertical: a lower role on a higher-privilege function.

flashcards.q: Which TLS versions are acceptable?
flashcards.a: TLS 1.2 or later with 1.3 preferred (RFC 8446). TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996).

flashcards.q: Name common cryptography misuse patterns.
flashcards.a: ECB mode, repeated nonces or IVs, MD5 or SHA-1 for security purposes, home-made algorithms and certificate validation switched off in code.

flashcards.q: What is the EICAR file for?
flashcards.a: A harmless antivirus test file used to check malware scanning at upload, mail and endpoint.

flashcards.q: How do you test an intrusion-detection rule?
flashcards.a: Run agreed, harmless attack simulations in a lab (for example Atomic Red Team) and check the rule fires, the alert is routed and someone responds.

flashcards.q: Why test egress as well as ingress?
flashcards.a: Unrestricted outbound traffic is how stolen data leaves.

flashcards.q: What does 'effective' mean for a security mechanism?
flashcards.a: A test shows it works. ISTQB asks testers to check effectiveness, not merely existence.

flashcards.q: How do you test data obfuscation?
flashcards.a: Inspect non-production data and logs, try re-identification by combining fields, and check reversibility and key handling.

flashcards.q: How strong must MFA recovery be?
flashcards.a: No weaker than the main login, otherwise attackers use recovery.

flashcards.q: What does hardening testing compare against?
flashcards.a: A baseline such as a CIS Benchmark or a vendor guide.

flashcards.q: How do you test for account enumeration?
flashcards.a: Compare messages and response timing for known and unknown users on login and reset; they must be identical.

flashcards.q: What is OWASP MASVS?
flashcards.a: The Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, with eight control groups. MASTG is the matching testing guide.

flashcards.q: Where should a mobile app keep credentials and tokens?
flashcards.a: In the platform keystore, not in preferences, files, logs or backups.

flashcards.q: When do root and jailbreak detection tests matter?
flashcards.a: Only for apps whose threat model needs them; test them against that model, not by default.

flashcards.q: What do you do first in cloud testing?
flashcards.a: Read the provider's penetration-testing policy, then start with identity: who can assume which role, old keys, wildcard permissions and administrator MFA.

flashcards.q: How does the shared responsibility model help a tester?
flashcards.a: It places each finding as provider-owned, customer-configured or application-level.

flashcards.q: Why is the instance metadata service a target?
flashcards.a: If it allows unauthenticated token retrieval, an attacker who reaches it can steal workload credentials.

flashcards.q: Why should cloud logs go to a separate account?
flashcards.a: So the workload cannot alter them.

flashcards.q: What do you check in container images?
flashcards.a: Known vulnerabilities and unwanted contents; prefer minimal base images and non-root users.

flashcards.q: Which runtime settings do you review for containers?
flashcards.a: No privileged containers, dropped capabilities, read-only file systems where possible and resource limits.

flashcards.q: Which Kubernetes areas do you review?
flashcards.a: RBAC, network policies, secret handling, Pod Security Admission levels and admission-control policies.

flashcards.q: What is configuration drift and how do you find it?
flashcards.a: The deployed state diverging from the infrastructure-as-code definition; compare deployed state with the code.

flashcards.q: How should you test operational technology?
flashcards.a: Prefer passive observation and agreed maintenance windows; active scanning can stop equipment.

flashcards.q: How do you test network segmentation?
flashcards.a: Try to cross each zone boundary from the less-trusted side, with default deny in mind.

flashcards.q: Which standards guide container and OT security?
flashcards.a: NIST SP 800-190 and the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark for containers; IEC 62443 and MITRE ATT&CK for ICS for operational technology.

flashcards.q: Why does LLM security differ from classic application security?
flashcards.a: Text is both data and instruction, so anyone who controls text the model reads may steer it. Test the whole system, not only the model.

flashcards.q: List the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025).
flashcards.a: LLM01 Prompt Injection, 02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, 03 Supply Chain, 04 Data and Model Poisoning, 05 Improper Output Handling, 06 Excessive Agency, 07 System Prompt Leakage, 08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, 09 Misinformation, 10 Unbounded Consumption.

flashcards.q: What controls reduce prompt-injection impact?
flashcards.a: Separate privileges, treat model output as untrusted and require human approval for high-impact actions.

flashcards.q: What is improper output handling (LLM05)?
flashcards.a: Downstream code interprets model output such as markup or commands. Encode and validate it like any untrusted input.

flashcards.q: What is excessive agency (LLM06)?
flashcards.a: The agent has tools or permissions beyond what is needed or beyond the caller's own rights. Use least privilege, narrow tools, user-scoped credentials and a human in the loop.

flashcards.q: Why report a success rate for LLM attacks?
flashcards.a: Outputs vary, so run each attack many times and report a rate; keep the set as a regression suite across model and prompt versions.

flashcards.q: Name three tools for LLM red teaming.
flashcards.a: garak, PyRIT and promptfoo.

flashcards.q: Which frameworks apply to AI systems?
flashcards.a: MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF with the Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1), ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act.

flashcards.q: What is the control for system prompt leakage (LLM07)?
flashcards.a: Keep secrets out of prompts and enforce rules outside the prompt.

flashcards.q: How do you test vector stores and retrieval?
flashcards.a: Test cross-tenant retrieval, injected documents and leakage from embeddings; enforce access control on the vector store.

flashcards.q: How did the Digital Omnibus change EU AI Act dates?
flashcards.a: Annex III high-risk obligations move from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 and Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028. Parliament approved it on 16 June 2026; confirm the final text.

flashcards.q: What AI techniques did ATT&CK v20 add?
flashcards.a: Direct and indirect prompt injection and AI-enabled exfiltration, among others.

flashcards.q: Why do attackers target people?
flashcards.a: Persuading a person is cheaper than defeating a technical control.

flashcards.q: Name the persuasion levers social engineers use.
flashcards.a: Authority, urgency, scarcity, social proof, reciprocity, liking and commitment.

flashcards.q: What controls reduce phishing?
flashcards.a: Mail filtering, phishing-resistant MFA, a report button and training.

flashcards.q: What is vishing and how is it controlled?
flashcards.a: Voice phishing, including help-desk impersonation. Use call-back verification and scripted identity checks.

flashcards.q: What is baiting?
flashcards.a: A lure such as a found USB stick or QR code. Controls: port control, device policy and awareness.

flashcards.q: What is tailgating and what must a physical test carry?
flashcards.a: Following an authorised person through a door. Physical tests need a signed authorisation letter carried at all times.

flashcards.q: What is business email compromise and how do you control it?
flashcards.a: An impersonated executive or supplier asks for a payment or data. Use out-of-band verification and dual approval.

flashcards.q: What is MFA fatigue and how do you control it?
flashcards.a: Repeated push prompts until someone approves. Use number matching, rate limits and phishing-resistant MFA; test the configuration, not the staff.

flashcards.q: How do you test deepfake risk ethically?
flashcards.a: With a tabletop exercise, using verification codes and call-back procedures as controls.

flashcards.q: Which metrics show whether awareness training works?
flashcards.a: Behaviour: report rate and time to report matter more than click rate; compare before and after and track repeat failures.

flashcards.q: What are the rules for testing people?
flashcards.a: Written leadership approval (legal and HR involved), defined data collection, aggregate reporting, no name and shame, no lures that exploit real distress, stop conditions and a debrief.

flashcards.q: Which controls limit insider risk?
flashcards.a: Least privilege, separation of duties, activity logging, data-loss prevention and a leaver process.

flashcards.q: How does a penetration test differ from a vulnerability assessment?
flashcards.a: An assessment is broad and mostly automated; a penetration test is deep within scope, time-boxed and proves impact.

flashcards.q: How does a red team differ from a purple team?
flashcards.a: A red team is goal-based and often covert and tests detection and response; a purple team is collaborative, attackers and defenders sharing each step.

flashcards.q: What are the penetration-test phases in NIST SP 800-115?
flashcards.a: Planning, discovery, attack and reporting.

flashcards.q: What are the PTES phases?
flashcards.a: Pre-engagement, intelligence gathering, threat modelling, vulnerability analysis, exploitation, post-exploitation and reporting.

flashcards.q: What is OSSTMM?
flashcards.a: ISECOM's metrics-driven method across human, physical, wireless, telecommunications and data-network channels.

flashcards.q: What are the CVSS v4.0 metric groups and score names?
flashcards.a: Base, Threat, Environmental and Supplemental; scores are named CVSS-B, CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE and CVSS-BTE.

flashcards.q: What changed in CVSS v4.0 compared with 3.1?
flashcards.a: Adds Attack Requirements, splits User Interaction into passive and active, retires Scope and rates impact for the vulnerable system and subsequent systems separately.

flashcards.q: What are the CVSS qualitative bands?
flashcards.a: None 0.0, low 0.1 to 3.9, medium 4.0 to 6.9, high 7.0 to 8.9, critical 9.0 to 10.0.

flashcards.q: What does EPSS estimate?
flashcards.a: The probability that a vulnerability is exploited within 30 days.

flashcards.q: What is the CISA KEV catalogue?
flashcards.a: A list of vulnerabilities with observed exploitation.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between CVE and CWE?
flashcards.a: A CVE names one specific disclosed vulnerability; a CWE names a type of weakness. CWE classifies and does not set priority.

flashcards.q: Why should you not prioritise by CVSS Base score alone?
flashcards.a: It is not risk and ignores your environment. Combine severity, likelihood (EPSS), observed exploitation (KEV), asset criticality and exposure.

flashcards.q: What is a security.txt file?
flashcards.a: A file giving security contact details for researchers, defined in RFC 9116.

flashcards.q: Which standards describe vulnerability disclosure and handling?
flashcards.a: ISO/IEC 29147 (disclosure) and ISO/IEC 30111 (handling).

flashcards.q: What belongs in a good penetration test report?
flashcards.a: Executive summary and scope and method; per finding a title, description, evidence, affected assets, impact, likelihood, CVSS vector and score, CWE, remediation and references.

flashcards.q: What are the stages of an engagement?
flashcards.a: Pre-engagement, information gathering and analysis, exploitation and post-exploitation, clean-up, then reporting and retest.

flashcards.q: Name the links of the detection chain.
flashcards.a: Telemetry, collection and integrity, detection rules, triage and response, and tooling health.

flashcards.q: What should a security log record carry?
flashcards.a: Actor, time, target and result, with no secrets.

flashcards.q: What are the logging hygiene rules?
flashcards.a: No secrets or full personal data, neutralise user input before logging (log injection), add correlation IDs, keep security logs apart from debug noise.

flashcards.q: What is Sigma?
flashcards.a: A shared, vendor-neutral format for detection rules, often mapped to ATT&CK techniques.

flashcards.q: What is Atomic Red Team used for?
flashcards.a: Running small, harmless simulations of techniques in a lab to check that detection rules fire.

flashcards.q: What is NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3?
flashcards.a: Incident response guidance published 3 April 2025 as a CSF 2.0 community profile; it supersedes Rev. 2 (2012).

flashcards.q: What are the classic incident-response phases of Rev. 2?
flashcards.a: Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity.

flashcards.q: How does response map to CSF 2.0 in the hub's reading?
flashcards.a: Response work sits mostly in Detect, Respond and Recover, with Govern, Identify and Protect supporting preparation.

flashcards.q: List the vulnerability management cycle.
flashcards.a: Inventory, assess, prioritise, remediate or mitigate, verify and report.

flashcards.q: What is the 3-2-1 backup idea?
flashcards.a: Three copies, two media types, one off-site, with at least one copy offline or immutable.

flashcards.q: When does a backup count?
flashcards.a: Only after a restore has worked. Schedule restore drills and record the result.

flashcards.q: What are RPO and RTO?
flashcards.a: Recovery point objective is the most data you can lose; recovery time objective is the longest downtime you can accept. Test against them.

flashcards.q: Which blue-team metrics are worth tracking?
flashcards.a: Mean time to detect and contain, ATT&CK techniques with a tested detection, false-positive rate, fix-by compliance and restore success rate.

flashcards.q: Why hold a blameless post-incident review?
flashcards.a: To find root causes (5 Whys separates symptoms from causes) and turn them into tracked fixes and new detections.

flashcards.q: How do you test tooling health?
flashcards.a: Alert when a log source goes silent and retest after upgrades.

flashcards.q: Which six functions make up NIST CSF 2.0?
flashcards.a: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (published February 2024).

flashcards.q: How do ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 differ?
flashcards.a: 27001 holds the certifiable ISMS requirements; 27002 is the control catalogue (93 controls in 2022).

flashcards.q: What are the CIS Controls v8.1?
flashcards.a: Eighteen prioritised controls with implementation groups, a practical baseline.

flashcards.q: Which NIST SP 800-53 controls cover testing?
flashcards.a: CA-8 penetration testing, RA-5 vulnerability scanning and SA-11 developer testing. Identifiers not re-checked.

flashcards.q: What does PCI DSS requirement 11 ask for?
flashcards.a: Regular scans, penetration tests at least annually and after significant change, and segmentation tests.

flashcards.q: What do GDPR Articles 32 and 33 say?
flashcards.a: Article 32 expects security appropriate to the risk, including regular testing of its effectiveness; Article 33 sets 72-hour breach notification to the regulator.

flashcards.q: What are the NIS2 incident reporting steps?
flashcards.a: An early warning within 24 hours, a notification at 72 hours and a final report after one month.

flashcards.q: What does DORA require for testing?
flashcards.a: A resilience testing programme, with threat-led penetration testing for designated entities at least every three years. DORA has applied since 17 January 2025.

flashcards.q: What does the EU Cyber Resilience Act require from 11 September 2026?
flashcards.a: Manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents: early warning in 24 hours, notification in 72 hours, final report 14 days after a fix (or one month for severe incidents).

flashcards.q: What is SOC 2?
flashcards.a: An AICPA attestation against the trust services criteria.

flashcards.q: Why is compliance 'the floor'?
flashcards.a: Passing a checklist shows conformance, not resistance, and testing only the checklist gives false assurance.

flashcards.q: What does a risk register hold?
flashcards.a: For each risk an owner, a treatment, a target date and the residual risk.

flashcards.q: How do test results feed the ISMS?
flashcards.a: As inputs to the risk register: a finding is a risk statement, not just a defect. ISO/IEC 27001 asks the organisation to improve its ISMS from such results.

flashcards.q: What evidence will an auditor ask for?
flashcards.a: Test plan, scope approval, results, defects and retest proof.

flashcards.q: Why test that detection and escalation meet legal clocks?
flashcards.a: Breach and vulnerability reporting windows start when you become aware of an event.

flashcards.q: Which categories does ISTQB use for security tools?
flashcards.a: White-box, black-box or grey-box, and static or dynamic.

flashcards.q: How should you select a security tool?
flashcards.a: From documented needs: risks, technologies and test levels; fit; quality of results (false positives and negatives on your own code, in a proof of concept); open-source risks; vendor capabilities; cost and skills.

flashcards.q: Name two intercepting web proxies.
flashcards.a: Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP.

flashcards.q: What are the common rollout traps for security tools?
flashcards.a: Every rule on at once; unauthenticated scans; scans that disrupt fragile systems; the tool itself as a supply-chain target; treating output as a verdict instead of a lead.

flashcards.q: Which tools scan for secrets?
flashcards.a: Gitleaks, TruffleHog and detect-secrets.

flashcards.q: Which tools generate or scan SBOMs and dependencies?
flashcards.a: Syft generates SBOMs; Grype, Trivy, OSV-Scanner and OWASP Dependency-Check find known vulnerable components.

flashcards.q: Which tools check TLS and hardening?
flashcards.a: testssl.sh and SSLyze for TLS; Lynis and OpenSCAP for hardening against baselines.

flashcards.q: Name three fuzzers.
flashcards.a: AFL++, libFuzzer and Jazzer.

flashcards.q: Which tools support mobile testing?
flashcards.a: MobSF, jadx, apktool, Frida and objection.

flashcards.q: Which tools check cloud posture?
flashcards.a: Prowler, ScoutSuite and Steampipe.

flashcards.q: How do you run OWASP Juice Shop safely on your machine?
flashcards.a: With Docker bound to localhost: docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop.

flashcards.q: Name the lab-safety rules.
flashcards.a: Isolated network, bind labs to localhost, snapshots, treat downloaded VMs and images as untrusted, separate attack VM, stay inside platform rules and never aim lab techniques at systems you do not own.

flashcards.q: Which two labs did the hub check in October 2026, and what did it find?
flashcards.a: PortSwigger Web Security Academy is described on its site as 100% free; OWASP Juice Shop is MIT-licensed, version 20.2.0.

flashcards.q: Which lab is a deliberately vulnerable API?
flashcards.a: OWASP crAPI.

questions.stem: An attacker changes the total on an order in transit and nobody notices. Which security property was violated?
options: Availability
Confidentiality
Integrity
Accountability
questions.explanation: Integrity means information cannot change without authorisation or without detection. An order total altered in transit is an attack on integrity, not on confidentiality (reading) or availability (use).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a threat from a vulnerability?
options: A threat is a weakness in software; a vulnerability is the attacker who uses it.
A threat is a confirmed breach; a vulnerability is a possible breach.
They mean the same thing; vulnerability is only the technical term.
A threat is a potential cause of harm; a vulnerability is a weakness a threat can use.
questions.explanation: A threat is described by actor, capability and intent; a vulnerability is the weakness it can use, and an exploit is the way of using it.

questions.stem: A login form answers 'Unknown user' for a name that does not exist and 'Wrong password' for one that does. Which property is mainly weakened?
options: Integrity, because an attacker can then alter the stored password records
Availability, because the two messages make logins slower
Confidentiality, because the response reveals which accounts exist
Non-repudiation, because user actions can no longer be traced
questions.explanation: This is account enumeration: the difference leaks information about users. The expected result is the same message and similar timing for both cases.

questions.stem: Which design principle says that when a component fails, access is denied rather than granted?
options: Security by obscurity
Complete mediation
Least privilege
Fail securely
questions.explanation: Failing securely means failing closed. Complete mediation is about checking every access, not about error behaviour.

questions.stem: In a finance tool, one clerk can both create and approve refunds. Which principle is violated?
options: Separation of duties
Fail securely
Complete mediation
Defence in depth
questions.explanation: Separation of duties means no single person can complete a sensitive action alone. One clerk who both creates and approves a refund can commit fraud unseen, so approval should need a second person.

questions.stem: How do a security audit and a security test relate?
options: They complement each other: audits check conformance, tests check resistance
An audit replaces testing whenever the standard is mandatory for the whole system
A test replaces an audit, because testing is more technical and finds more
They are the same activity, and the two names come from different teams
questions.explanation: An audit checks conformance to a policy; a test tries to show whether controls resist an attack scenario.

questions.stem: In the AAA trio, which element records what an actor did?
options: Authentication
Accounting
Availability
Authorization
questions.explanation: Authentication is who you are, authorization is what you may do, accounting is what you did.

questions.stem: A company has a strong perimeter firewall but a flat internal network. One phished laptop leads to the customer database. Which missing idea best explains how far the attack spread?
options: Defence in depth, with verification inside the network as zero trust asks
Security by obscurity, hiding the internal hosts from view
Fail securely, so that a crashed component never grants access
Non-repudiation, proving which user performed each action
questions.explanation: Once past the perimeter there was no independent internal layer. Zero trust says not to grant access because of network location.

questions.stem: Which expression gives risk in its simplest form?
options: The technical severity score of the vulnerability on its own
Likelihood multiplied by impact for a specific scenario
The number of vulnerabilities found by the latest scan
The total cost of the security controls in the budget
questions.explanation: Risk is judged per scenario, not per vulnerability, and combines how likely and how costly it is.

questions.stem: Which ISTQB certificate launched in February 2025 as a successor to the 2016 Security Tester syllabus?
options: CT-STE, Security Test Engineer
CTFL v4.0.1, Foundation Level
CTAL-TM, Advanced Level Test Manager
CT-AI, Certified Tester AI Testing
questions.explanation: CT-STE launched in February 2025 and, together with a planned CT-STA, replaces the 2016 CT-SEC syllabus. CTFL is the Foundation prerequisite, not a security successor.

questions.stem: How many points are needed to pass the CT-STE exam?
options: 26 of 40 points (65%)
52 of 80 points (65%)
28 of 43 points (65%)
30 of 43 points (70%)
questions.explanation: CT-STE has 40 questions worth 43 points in 75 minutes. 26 of 40 is the CTFL pass mark and 52 of 80 is the CT-SEC pass mark.

questions.stem: Which statement about holders of the legacy CT-SEC certificate is correct?
options: They are automatically awarded CT-STE because the new syllabus covers the same content
They keep CT-SEC and automatically receive CT-STA as soon as that exam is released
There is no grandfathering: they must pass the CT-STE or CT-STA exam to hold those titles
They receive CT-STE after paying a conversion fee and submitting their old CT-SEC certificate
questions.explanation: ISTQB states there is no grandfathering. CT-SEC holders keep their CT-SEC certificate, but nothing converts automatically, so they must pass the CT-STE or CT-STA exam to hold those titles.

questions.stem: What is the prerequisite for taking the CT-STE exam?
options: The ISTQB Certified Tester Foundation Level (CTFL)
CTFL plus three years of security experience
An advanced-level ISTQB certificate
CISSP
questions.explanation: CT-STE requires the Foundation Level (CTFL). The extra three years of experience belonged to the older CT-SEC requirement and does not apply here.

questions.stem: Which theme has its own chapter in the 2016 CT-SEC syllabus but not in CT-STE v1.0.1?
options: Standards and best practices
Human factors in security testing
Reporting security test results
Security testing tools
questions.explanation: CT-SEC chapter 6 covers human factors; CT-STE has no dedicated chapter for it.

questions.stem: At which K-level are keywords and security domain-specific terms examinable in CT-STE?
options: K4, analyse
K2, understand
K1, remember
K3, apply
questions.explanation: CT-STE makes all keywords and security domain-specific terms examinable at K1.

questions.stem: What do standards primarily give a security tester, in ISTQB's view?
options: Guaranteed protection against attacks for every system that follows them
A mandatory list of tools that every tester has to purchase and install
Test oracles (what correct means), a shared vocabulary and audit evidence
Legal immunity while testing, as long as the standard is cited in the plan
questions.explanation: Standards define 'correct'. Mandatory ones come from regulation or contract, voluntary ones are chosen as good practice.

questions.stem: A CT-STE candidate has 75 minutes for 40 questions. Which plan fits?
options: Answer the sure ones first, flag the rest and budget about 1.9 minutes per question
Spend five minutes on each question and skip whatever is left at the end
Read every question twice before answering any, then start from the last one
Answer only the K1 questions and leave the other levels blank
questions.explanation: 75 minutes divided by 40 questions is about 1.9 minutes each; flagging protects the time.

questions.stem: Which five stages does the 2016 CT-SEC syllabus define for the security test process?
options: Planning, design, execution, evaluation and maintenance
Discovery, exploitation, escalation, persistence and reporting
Identify, protect, detect, respond and recover
Preparation, detection, containment, eradication and recovery
questions.explanation: The others are a penetration-test lifecycle, the older five CSF functions and the incident-response lifecycle.

questions.stem: Which order shows the stages of the security test process?
options: Scan, exploit, report, retest, close
Plan, design, execute, evaluate, maintain
Plan, execute, design, report, close
Design, plan, execute, maintain, evaluate
questions.explanation: The process runs plan, design, execute, evaluate, maintain. Planning comes first because it fixes scope, approvals and risks, and maintain closes the loop by keeping the tests current.

questions.stem: Why does the Plan stage decide whether the later stages are legal and safe?
options: It selects the scanner, and a bought scanner makes later tests legal
It is where the exploit code is written and approved by management
It is the only stage that produces evidence for the final report
It produces the signed authorisation, scope and rules of engagement
questions.explanation: Without signed written authorisation naming the tester, targets and dates, no test should run. The Plan stage also fixes scope and rules of engagement, so it decides whether later stages are legal and safe.

questions.stem: A test lead ranks four scenarios. Which should get the deepest testing first? Invoice read by another customer (likelihood high, impact high); credential stuffing (high, medium); stored script in a comment field (medium, medium); outdated library with a known flaw (medium, medium).
options: A stored script in a comment field
A customer reads another customer's invoice
An outdated library with a known flaw
Credential stuffing on login
questions.explanation: Risk-based testing ranks scenarios by likelihood and impact. The invoice read is rated high on both, so it gets the deepest testing first; credential stuffing is high likelihood but only medium impact.

questions.stem: The lockout threshold is 5 failed logins. Which tests best apply boundary value analysis?
options: 1, 10 and 100 failed logins
5 failed logins spread over five accounts
6 failed logins only
4, 5 and 6 consecutive failed logins
questions.explanation: Boundary tests sit at N-1, N and N+1, and also confirm that the real user can recover.

questions.stem: Which ISTQB technique best finds a flaw where a password-reset link still works after the password was changed?
options: Statement coverage
Equivalence partitioning
Boundary value analysis
State transition testing
questions.explanation: A reset link that survives a password change breaks the intended order of states. State transition testing attacks out-of-order, replayed and reused steps, which techniques working on input values (equivalence partitioning, boundary values) do not target.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of an exit criterion for a security test?
options: The scanner reports zero findings on its last run against the test environment
The planned number of test days has passed, whatever was covered by then
All high-priority scenarios executed; no critical finding open without risk acceptance
All executed tests passed on the first run, so no retest was needed
questions.explanation: Exit criteria tie to risk coverage and the handling of findings, not to the tool or the calendar.

questions.stem: A tester must show that each role can or cannot perform each action on each object type. Which technique fits?
options: Decision table testing
Equivalence partitioning of passwords
Fuzzing
Exploratory testing
questions.explanation: A role x action x object matrix is a decision table; automate it for regression.

questions.stem: During execution a tester finds real customer records in the test environment. What is the best response?
options: Keep using them, because real data makes the test results more realistic
Paste a few of the records into the report as proof of the exposure
