Stop using them, report it and continue with masked or synthetic data
Copy them to a personal spreadsheet and anonymise them there first
questions.explanation: Real customer data in a test environment is a privacy and compliance problem: stop using it, report it and continue with masked or synthetic data, without copying it anywhere else.

questions.stem: A report lists 80 'critical' findings copied from a scanner, none manually verified. Which weakness in the Evaluate stage does this show?
options: Tool output was treated as a verdict, without verification or a severity rationale
The report was marked too confidential for the stakeholders to act on it
The scanner was open source, so its findings cannot be trusted
Too few of the tests were automated, so the scanner covered too little
questions.explanation: Tool output is a lead, not a verdict. Verify each finding and justify severity.

questions.stem: Against what is security test coverage measured?
options: Lines of code executed by the functional test suite, as for any other test type
The number of security tools run in the pipeline and how often they ran
Concrete items: threat-model elements, requirements, ASVS or Top 10 categories
The number of hours the testers spent on the system during the project
questions.explanation: Without a concrete reference, 'coverage' cannot show what was left untested.

questions.stem: Which test type probes the running application from outside?
options: SAST
Secret scanning
SCA
DAST
questions.explanation: DAST (dynamic application security testing) sends requests to the running application from outside. SAST and SCA analyse code and components without running anything, and secret scanning searches repositories.

questions.stem: Which defect is a SAST tool least likely to find?
options: A call to an unsafe or deprecated library function
A business-logic flaw such as skipping a checkout step
A SQL query string built by concatenating raw user input
A hard-coded password stored in a source code file
questions.explanation: SAST reads code patterns such as concatenated SQL, hard-coded secrets and unsafe APIs. A business-logic flaw like skipping a checkout step belongs to the workflow, which needs design review, dynamic tests and manual testing.

questions.stem: What does software composition analysis report?
options: How the running application behaves when it is attacked
Weak or reused passwords in the production user database
Business-logic flaws in the code your own team wrote
Known-vulnerable third-party components and their licence issues
questions.explanation: Software composition analysis matches your component inventory against vulnerability databases and licence data. It does not find flaws in your own code or in runtime behaviour.

questions.stem: Developers ignore a pipeline gate that fails on every old finding in the backlog. Which change keeps the gate useful?
options: Lower the severity of every old finding so the gate stops failing
Block only on new, high-confidence, high-severity findings in changed code
Run the gate only once a month instead of on every single change, to reduce noise
Disable scanning in feature branches and scan only the main branch
questions.explanation: A gate that fails on every old finding is always red and gets switched off. Gate on new findings in changed code, block only on high-confidence, high-severity results, and work the backlog separately.

questions.stem: What is an SBOM?
options: A signed approval that allows the team to run security tests
A machine-readable list of the components inside software
A summary report of all penetration tests done on the system
A backup copy of the source code kept in a separate location
questions.explanation: An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of the components in software, in formats such as SPDX or CycloneDX, so you can find affected products quickly when a component is disclosed as vulnerable.

questions.stem: Which security activity belongs at the Design stage?
options: Dependency scanning of the nightly build
Threat modelling and secure design review
Authenticated DAST against the staging site
Applying emergency patches in production
questions.explanation: At the Design stage, threat modelling and secure design review find flaws before any code exists. Check that each threat has a mitigation and each mitigation has a test.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a shift-right control?
options: A security requirements workshop with the product owner
Pre-commit secret scanning on every developer laptop
Threat modelling during the design stage of a feature
Production monitoring with a disclosure channel and bug bounty
questions.explanation: Shift-right adds controls after release; shift-left alone is a listed failure mode.

questions.stem: A team runs SAST, SCA and DAST in CI and sees no serious findings, yet a penetration test shows users reading each other's invoices. What best explains the gap?
options: The penetration tester used a faster scanner with newer detection rules
Invoices are outside the OWASP Top 10, so scanners never look at them
Scanners rarely detect authorization flaws and role-by-object tests were missing
SAST must have been disabled, because DAST alone would catch this flaw
questions.explanation: Treating scanner output as the test is a named failure mode; keep scripted and manual authorization tests.

questions.stem: Which framework is a maturity model scored across five business functions?
options: CIS Controls
NIST SSDF
OWASP SAMM
SLSA
questions.explanation: SAMM scores governance, design, implementation, verification and operations.

questions.stem: Which category is first in OWASP Top 10:2025?
options: A04 Cryptographic Failures
A02 Security Misconfiguration
A01 Broken Access Control
A05 Injection
questions.explanation: Broken Access Control is A01 in the 2025 list, as in 2021. Security Misconfiguration rose to A02, while Cryptographic Failures fell to A04 and Injection to A05.

questions.stem: Where was server-side request forgery placed in the 2025 Top 10?
options: Merged into A02 Security Misconfiguration
Merged into A01 Broken Access Control
Kept as its own A10
Merged into A05 Injection
questions.explanation: In the 2025 list SSRF is no longer its own category: it was folded into A01 Broken Access Control. A10 in 2025 is the new Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

questions.stem: Which OWASP resource explains how to test web applications?
options: The Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG)
The Top 10, the list of the most critical risks
ASVS, the Application Security Verification Standard
SAMM, the Software Assurance Maturity Model
questions.explanation: Top 10 raises awareness, ASVS lists requirements, WSTG explains how to test.

questions.stem: A tester changes /invoice/1001 to /invoice/1002 and sees another customer's invoice. Which Top 10:2025 category is this?
options: A01 Broken Access Control
A04 Cryptographic Failures
A05 Injection
A07 Authentication Failures
questions.explanation: Changing an identifier to read someone else's record is an insecure direct object reference, which is an access-control failure (A01); in API terms it is BOLA. No authentication or injection flaw is involved.

questions.stem: A session cookie lacks the HttpOnly flag. Which risk increases?
options: The cookie can be sent over plain HTTP connections
The cookie is also sent along with requests to other sites
The cookie never expires, even after the user logs out
Script injected through XSS can read the cookie
questions.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from script; Secure and SameSite address the other risks.

questions.stem: A query is built by concatenating user input. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: A longer input length limit
Parameterised queries
Hiding database error messages
Blocking the word SELECT
questions.explanation: Parameterised queries keep data and code apart, which removes the root cause. Length limits, hidden errors and keyword blocking are weak, bypassable layers at best.

questions.stem: What does ASVS provide?
options: A catalogue of common weakness types with numbered identifiers
A ranked list of the ten most common application risks
Testable requirements grouped into three verification levels
A step-by-step guide for running each type of scan
questions.explanation: ASVS lists testable requirements at three verification levels; choose a level per application from its risk. It is not a scan guide (that is WSTG), a weakness catalogue (CWE) or the Top 10 list.

questions.stem: An upload form accepts invoice.pdf.php and stores it in the web root where it can be requested. Which controls address this?
options: Check the file extension in client-side JavaScript before the upload
Rename uploaded files to lower case and keep them in the web root
Check content type on the server, store outside the web root, never execute uploads
Raise the maximum upload size so that legitimate invoices are accepted
questions.explanation: Client-side checks can be bypassed, so the server must decide: check the content, store files outside the web root and never execute uploads. A double extension such as .pdf.php is the classic trick.

questions.stem: The application lets requests through when its policy service is unavailable. Which Top 10:2025 category fits best?
options: A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures
A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures
A07 Authentication Failures
questions.explanation: Failing open is a classic exceptional-condition flaw; the secure behaviour is to fail closed.

questions.stem: Which change did the 2025 Top 10 make compared with 2021?
options: Injection moved up from third place to first place
Cryptographic Failures rose from second place to first place
Insecure Design was removed from the list altogether
Security Misconfiguration rose from fifth to second place
questions.explanation: Injection fell from third to fifth and Cryptographic Failures from second to fourth.

questions.stem: What is API1:2023?
options: Broken Object Level Authorization
Server Side Request Forgery
Broken Authentication
Unrestricted Resource Consumption
questions.explanation: API1:2023 is Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), the first entry in the 2023 API list. SSRF is API7, Broken Authentication is API2 and Unrestricted Resource Consumption is API4.

questions.stem: A profile update accepts a role field set to admin and the user becomes an administrator. Which API risk is this?
options: API9 Improper Inventory Management
API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
API5 Broken Function Level Authorization
API1 Broken Object Level Authorization
questions.explanation: Setting a protected property such as role through an update is mass assignment, covered by API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization. Writes must accept only allow-listed fields.

questions.stem: An ordinary user can successfully call an administrative delete endpoint. Which API risk is this?
options: API5 Broken Function Level Authorization
API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
API7 Server Side Request Forgery
questions.explanation: Calling an administrative function as an ordinary user is Broken Function Level Authorization (API5). The server must check the role for each function, not merely hide the button.

questions.stem: Why are random UUID object identifiers not a fix for BOLA?
options: Unguessable IDs are not access control; each handler must still check ownership
UUIDs are slower to compare, which opens a timing side channel
UUIDs are not permitted in REST URLs under the OWASP guidance
UUIDs can be decrypted back into the underlying database row numbers
questions.explanation: IDs leak through lists, logs and shared links; the server must check access.

questions.stem: A script books thousands of appointments through a legitimate flow to block competitors. Which API risk is this?
options: API2 Broken Authentication, because the script logs in repeatedly
API8 Security Misconfiguration of the booking service
API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIs from third-party providers
API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
questions.explanation: Abusing a legitimate flow at scale, such as booking slots to block competitors, is API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows. Identify the sensitive flows, then limit and monitor them.

questions.stem: A webhook-setup parameter makes the server request an internal address supplied by the caller. Which risk is being tested?
options: API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
API7 Server Side Request Forgery
API9 Improper Inventory Management
API8 Security Misconfiguration
questions.explanation: Making the server fetch a caller-supplied internal address is API7 Server Side Request Forgery. Control it with destination allow-lists and by blocking internal address ranges.

questions.stem: Which approach gives systematic coverage of API authorization?
options: A review of the OpenAPI file alone, without sending requests
One smoke test per endpoint using a single admin account
A DAST scan run with default settings and no test accounts
A role x endpoint x object matrix, automated with scripts
questions.explanation: A role x endpoint x object matrix is a decision table: it covers every combination systematically, and scripts or a proxy extension make it repeatable. A default scan or one smoke test per endpoint misses object-level checks.

questions.stem: Which checks belong to JWT validation?
options: Only that the token is Base64 encoded and under 4 KB
Only the expiry, because a signed token cannot be forged or replayed
Only the issuer, because the other claims are advisory
Signature, algorithm allow-list, issuer, audience and expiry
questions.explanation: Validate every claim you rely on: the signature, an algorithm allow-list, the issuer, the audience and the expiry. Checking only one of them leaves forged or misdirected tokens working.

questions.stem: A GraphQL endpoint allows 500 login attempts in one request by aliasing the same mutation. Which control helps most?
options: Disable HTTPS between the gateway and the API for speed
Limit batching, aliasing and query complexity, and rate-limit by cost
Allow introspection in production so that clients can adapt
Increase the page size so that clients need fewer requests
questions.explanation: Aliasing and batching let an attacker pack many attempts into one request and dodge request-based rate limits. Limit them, bound query complexity and rate-limit by cost.

questions.stem: Which password policy is consistent with NIST SP 800-63B-4 for single-factor use?
options: Minimum 15 characters, no composition rules, breached-password check
A maximum length of 12 characters so that users can remember it
Minimum 8 characters with upper, lower, digit and symbol required
Forced rotation every 90 days, with a new password of at least 12 characters
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-63B-4 asks for at least 15 characters for single-factor passwords, forbids composition rules and forced periodic changes, and requires a check against breached passwords.

questions.stem: The policy requires at least 15 characters for single-factor passwords. Which two inputs best test the minimum?
options: A 14-character and a 15-character password
A 14-character and a 16-character password
A 1-character and a 100-character password
An 8-character and a 16-character password
questions.explanation: Boundary value analysis tests on both sides of the limit: 14 characters must be rejected and 15 accepted. The other pairs do not straddle the boundary.

questions.stem: After logout, the old session ID still returns the account page. Which check failed?
options: Idle timeout boundary on the session cookie
Cookie flag check for Secure and HttpOnly
Server-side session invalidation on logout
CSRF defence on the logout request
questions.explanation: Reusing an old session ID after logout and password change must be rejected.

questions.stem: Why test egress traffic as well as ingress?
options: Unrestricted outbound traffic is how stolen data leaves
Ingress rules cannot be tested without access to the provider
Egress traffic is slower, so it needs separate performance tests
Regulators only audit egress rules, never ingress rules
questions.explanation: Stolen data and command-and-control traffic leave through outbound paths, so default-deny egress filtering limits them. Ingress and egress rules are both testable, so test both.

questions.stem: A server still negotiates TLS 1.0. What is the right finding?
options: A finding only for servers that sit on the internal network
No finding at all as long as strong ciphers are negotiated
A deprecated protocol: disable it and require TLS 1.2 or later
A finding only if the certificate has also expired or is self-signed
questions.explanation: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated, so negotiating them is a finding whatever the certificate or cipher quality. Disable them, require TLS 1.2 or later and prefer 1.3.

questions.stem: What is the EICAR file used for?
options: A real ransomware sample used for analyst training
A tool for fuzzing file-upload endpoints with random bytes
A test certificate for checking TLS client handling
A harmless test file to check that malware scanning works
questions.explanation: The EICAR file is a harmless standard string that antivirus engines detect, so it shows that upload, mail and endpoint scanning works without using live malware.

questions.stem: A detection rule fires correctly, but the alert goes to a mailbox nobody reads. Which link of the detection chain failed?
options: Detection rules
Collection and integrity
Telemetry
Triage and response
questions.explanation: The rule fired, so telemetry and detection worked; the failure is in triage and response, because nobody reads the mailbox. A control that alerts nobody has failed.

questions.stem: Which is a cryptography misuse pattern?
options: Using TLS 1.3
Reusing a nonce or IV with the same key
Using AES-GCM with unique nonces
Hashing passwords with Argon2id and unique salts
questions.explanation: Other misuse patterns: ECB mode, MD5 or SHA-1 for security, home-made algorithms and disabled certificate validation.

questions.stem: What is a vertical authorization test?
options: Using the same role to reach another user's data record
Checking only that tenants cannot see each other's data
Using a lower-privileged role on a higher-privilege function
Testing which TLS ciphers a server will negotiate with clients
questions.explanation: A vertical test uses a lower-privileged role on a higher-privilege function. A horizontal test uses the same role on someone else's data.

questions.stem: Test-data masking replaced customer names but kept birth date, postcode and gender. What is the best analysis?
options: Quasi-identifiers allow re-identification, so the masking is not effective
Only names count as personal data, so the remaining fields are all harmless
Masking is effective, because the direct identifiers have been removed
Masking is effective as long as the masked database is also encrypted
questions.explanation: Birth date, postcode and gender are quasi-identifiers: combined they can single out a person, so the data is still personal. Test obfuscation by attempting re-identification across fields.

questions.stem: What is OWASP MASVS?
options: A verification standard for mobile apps with eight control groups
A catalogue of mobile malware families seen in app stores
A benchmark for hardening cloud accounts and services
A container runtime for running mobile app test builds
questions.explanation: MASVS, the Mobile Application Security Verification Standard, groups its controls into eight areas, and MASTG is the matching testing guide. It is not malware, a cloud benchmark or a runtime.

questions.stem: A mobile app stores its login token in a plain preferences file. Which control is missing?
options: A longer minimum password length
Storage in the platform keystore
Certificate pinning for API calls
Root and jailbreak detection
questions.explanation: Credentials and tokens belong in the platform keystore, which protects them at rest. A plain preferences file can be read from backups or by anything with file access; pinning and root detection do not fix storage.

questions.stem: What should you do first when testing a customer's cloud environment?
options: Test the provider's own management plane for design weaknesses and exposure
Read the provider's testing policy, confirm authorisation, then start with identity
Scan the provider's whole public address range to map the customer's tenant
Run exploit frameworks against the provider's shared services to gauge impact
questions.explanation: Providers publish testing rules that differ by service, so read the policy and confirm written authorisation first, then start with identity: who can assume which role. The provider's own platform and other tenants are out of scope.

questions.stem: A storage bucket is publicly readable because the customer configured it so. In the shared responsibility model this finding is...
options: Not a finding
Application-level
Provider-owned
Customer-configured
questions.explanation: Place each finding as provider-owned, customer-configured or application-level.

questions.stem: A container runs privileged as root with no resource limits. Which review area covers this?
options: Network segmentation
Image vulnerability scan
Runtime settings
RBAC review
questions.explanation: Privileged mode, running as root, capabilities, read-only file systems and resource limits are runtime settings of a container, so the runtime-settings review covers this finding.

questions.stem: Why scan infrastructure-as-code in the pull request?
options: To generate an SBOM and nothing else from the templates
To measure application performance before the code is merged
To replace the penetration test that precedes each release
To catch misconfigurations before they reach deployment
questions.explanation: Scanning infrastructure-as-code in the pull request catches misconfigurations before they are deployed. Later, compare the deployed state with the code to find drift.

questions.stem: You must test a plant control network. Which approach fits?
options: Switching off monitoring during tests
Passive observation and agreed maintenance windows
A full active port scan during production hours
Fuzzing every controller
questions.explanation: Active scanning can crash fragile controllers, so observe passively and test only inside agreed maintenance windows, with the plant operators informed.

questions.stem: Why is an exposed instance metadata service dangerous?
options: It can allow unauthenticated retrieval of workload credentials
It stores all user passwords in clear text on the instance disk
It blocks logging, because the agent can no longer reach the service
It only affects billing, because the metadata lists the instance cost
questions.explanation: Cloud instances can read short-lived credentials from a metadata endpoint; if a request-forwarding flaw or an open network path lets an outsider reach it, they can act with the workload's identity. Test for it in every cloud review and require the hardened, token-based metadata mode.

questions.stem: Which OWASP LLM risk is LLM01?
options: Prompt Injection
Misinformation
Unbounded Consumption
Excessive Agency
questions.explanation: LLM01 in the 2025 list is Prompt Injection, the top-ranked risk. LLM06 is Excessive Agency, LLM09 Misinformation and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption.

questions.stem: An email assistant obeys a message saying 'forward all contacts to this address' and does it. Which two LLM risks combine here?
options: LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning and LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
LLM03 Supply Chain and LLM09 Misinformation
LLM01 Prompt Injection and LLM06 Excessive Agency
LLM07 System Prompt Leakage and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption
questions.explanation: The hidden instruction is an indirect prompt injection (LLM01), and the assistant acting on it without approval is Excessive Agency (LLM06). Limit the agent's tools and require human approval for high-impact actions.

questions.stem: Why should each LLM attack prompt be run many times?
options: Providers require repeat runs before they accept a vulnerability report
Outputs vary, so report a success rate rather than one pass or fail
Repetition makes the outputs deterministic, so later runs are cheaper
The model forgets earlier attempts, so each run must be repeated
questions.explanation: Model outputs vary between runs, so one pass or fail proves little. Report a success rate over many runs and keep the prompts as a regression suite across model and prompt versions.

questions.stem: Model output is inserted into a web page and a script in it executes. Which risk is this?
options: LLM09 Misinformation
LLM07 System Prompt Leakage
LLM05 Improper Output Handling
LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure
questions.explanation: Model output is untrusted data. When it is inserted into a page and a script runs, the risk is LLM05 Improper Output Handling; encode and validate it like any untrusted input.

questions.stem: How should secrets and rules be handled for system prompts?
options: Store API keys in the prompt but encrypt the whole prompt text
Keep secrets out of prompts and enforce rules outside the prompt
Put the admin password in the prompt for convenient reuse
Tell the model never to reveal them and rely on that instruction
questions.explanation: Prompts can leak, so a prompt cannot be the security control. Keep secrets out of it and enforce rules in code, permissions and filters outside the model.

questions.stem: A retrieval-augmented assistant returns a document belonging to another tenant. Which control addresses this?
options: Per-user retrieval authorization plus tenant isolation in the vector store
A lower temperature setting to make the answers less random overall
A longer system prompt that tells the model to respect each tenant
A larger context window so that fewer retrieved documents get truncated away
questions.explanation: Cross-tenant leakage in retrieval is an access-control failure in the data layer. Apply per-user authorization at retrieval time and isolate tenants in the vector store; test cross-tenant queries and injected documents.

questions.stem: What is MITRE ATLAS?
options: A legal register of AI regulations adopted by national governments worldwide
A benchmark suite that scores large language models on reasoning
A public registry of trained AI models and their licences
A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems
questions.explanation: ATLAS is modelled on MITRE ATT&CK and catalogues tactics, techniques and real case studies for attacks on machine-learning and AI systems. It is a knowledge base, not a regulation, a benchmark or a model registry.

questions.stem: Under the Digital Omnibus approved by the European Parliament on 16 June 2026, when do the Annex III high-risk obligations apply?
options: 2 August 2028
2 August 2026
1 January 2030
2 December 2027
questions.explanation: Annex III high-risk obligations move to 2 December 2027, and Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028. Confirm the final published text.

questions.stem: Which metric best shows that awareness training changed behaviour?
options: Course attendance and completion rates
The number of simulated phishing emails sent
Click rate on simulated phishing emails alone
Report rate and time to report suspicious messages
questions.explanation: Measure behaviour, not attendance: a rising report rate and a shorter time to report show that people act on suspicious messages. Compare before and after, and use more than one metric.

questions.stem: An email that seems to come from the CEO asks finance to wire money urgently. Which control is most effective?
options: A longer minimum length in the password policy
Switching off spell-check in the mail client
Blocking all external email at the mail gateway
Out-of-band verification and dual approval for payments
questions.explanation: This is business email compromise (CEO fraud). The strongest defence is a process control that does not depend on spotting the fake: out-of-band verification, such as a call-back, plus dual approval.

questions.stem: A user receives dozens of push prompts at 3 a.m. and eventually approves one. Which control best reduces this?
options: Disabling MFA for staff who work the night shift
Number matching, rate limits and phishing-resistant MFA
Sending the approval prompt by SMS text message instead of the app
Stricter password complexity rules for every account
questions.explanation: This is MFA fatigue. Number matching, rate limits and phishing-resistant authenticators remove the habit of tapping approve; test the configuration, not the staff.

questions.stem: Which rule applies to phishing simulations?
options: Report results in aggregate and do not name and shame individuals
Use lures about layoffs and bonuses to make the test feel realistic
Collect the real passwords that users type, for later analysis
Publish click lists to line managers to motivate the team
questions.explanation: Report simulation results in aggregate and never name and shame individuals. Also avoid lures that exploit real distress, and never collect real passwords.

questions.stem: What must a physical tailgating test carry?
options: A cloned badge made from a real employee's card
A verbal OK from the security guard on duty
A signed authorisation letter carried at all times
Nothing at all, so that the test stays as realistic as possible
questions.explanation: A physical test needs signed written approval carried at all times, so the tester can prove authorisation to guards or police. A verbal OK or a cloned badge is not acceptable.

questions.stem: Which of these is a persuasion lever used in social engineering?
options: Encryption
Segmentation
Rate limiting
Urgency
questions.explanation: Others: authority, scarcity, social proof, reciprocity, liking and commitment.

questions.stem: Which test approach suits deepfake and business email compromise risks?
options: Live voice-cloning calls to executives without approval
A tabletop exercise or process walkthrough
Network port scanning
Mass phishing of all staff
questions.explanation: Deepfake and business-email-compromise risk lives in processes and verification steps, so test them with a tabletop exercise or walkthrough. Unapproved voice cloning or mass phishing is not an acceptable test.

questions.stem: Which controls limit insider risk?
options: Least privilege, separation of duties and a leaver process
Longer passwords as the only control for insiders
Removing audit logging to protect staff privacy
Shared administrator accounts for the whole team
questions.explanation: Least privilege, separation of duties and a leaver process limit what an insider can do and for how long. Add activity logging and data-loss prevention.

questions.stem: Which assessment is goal-based, often covert and tests detection and response?
options: Red team
Vulnerability assessment
Bug bounty
Purple team
questions.explanation: A red team is goal-based and often covert, testing detection and response as well as prevention. A purple team is collaborative, and a vulnerability assessment is broad and mostly automated.

questions.stem: Which CVSS qualitative band covers scores 7.0 to 8.9?
options: Medium
Critical
Low
High
questions.explanation: CVSS qualitative bands: Low 0.1 to 3.9, Medium 4.0 to 6.9, High 7.0 to 8.9 and Critical 9.0 to 10.0.

questions.stem: What does EPSS estimate?
options: The number of hosts in the estate that are affected
The technical severity of the vulnerability itself
The date on which the vendor will release a patch
The probability of exploitation in the next 30 days
questions.explanation: EPSS estimates the probability that a vulnerability is exploited in the next 30 days. CVSS rates severity, and the KEV catalogue lists vulnerabilities with observed exploitation.

questions.stem: CVE A: CVSS 9.8, low EPSS, not in the KEV catalogue, isolated lab server. CVE B: CVSS 7.5, in the KEV catalogue, internet-facing production. Which first?
options: CVE A, because its Base score is higher than CVE B's
CVE B, because exploitation is observed and exposure is high
Both equally, because both are above the high severity threshold
Neither, until the EPSS score of CVE B is also high
questions.explanation: Combine severity, likelihood, observed exploitation and exposure. CVE B is in the KEV catalogue and internet-facing, so it is being attacked now; CVE A's higher Base score sits on an isolated lab server with low EPSS.

questions.stem: Which are the penetration-test phases in NIST SP 800-115?
options: Scan, exploit, persist and exfiltrate
Preparation, containment, eradication and recovery
Identify, protect, detect, respond and recover
Planning, discovery, attack and reporting
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-115 describes planning, discovery, attack and reporting. The other sequences are an incident-response lifecycle, the CSF functions and an attacker's activities.

questions.stem: What does a CWE identifier tell you?
options: The patch priority
The exploitation probability
A specific disclosed vulnerability
The type of weakness
questions.explanation: A CWE identifier names a type of weakness, such as CWE-79 for cross-site scripting. A CVE names one specific disclosed vulnerability; CWE says nothing about patch priority or exploitation probability.

questions.stem: Before testing a client application hosted by a cloud provider, which item must be settled?
options: Only a verbal agreement from the application owner's line manager
Written authorisation covering the app and its hosting providers
A Base score assigned for each finding expected in advance
Permission from the tester's own manager and nobody else
questions.explanation: Written authorisation must come from someone entitled to give it and must also cover third parties, because cloud and hosting providers often have their own testing rules.

questions.stem: What does the name CVSS-BTE mean?
options: A score using the Base, Threat and Environmental groups
A score using Base, Time and Exploit metric groups
A score using the Base and Temporal metric groups
A bug-tracking entry format that is used in scoring reports
questions.explanation: CVSS v4.0 names scores by the groups used: CVSS-B, CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE and CVSS-BTE, where B is Base, T is Threat and E is Environmental.

questions.stem: What is security.txt?
options: A signed penetration-test report
A scanner configuration
A file giving researchers security contact details
A list of known exploited vulnerabilities
questions.explanation: security.txt (RFC 9116) is a small text file, usually served at /.well-known/security.txt, that tells researchers whom to contact and how to report a vulnerability. It is a disclosure aid, not a report, a scanner setting or a vulnerability list.

questions.stem: A penetration-test report includes screenshots with real customer personal data and a full database dump as an appendix. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, because more evidence always makes the report stronger
Evidence should be minimal and sanitised, and the report treated as confidential
The screenshots should be in colour so that reviewers can read the data
The report should be made public so that other teams can learn from it
questions.explanation: Evidence should prove impact with the minimum necessary data: sanitise screenshots, never bulk-copy real sensitive data, and handle the report itself as confidential.

questions.stem: Which detection-chain link is tested by alerting when a log source goes silent?
options: Tooling health
Detection rules
Telemetry
Triage and response
questions.explanation: A silent log source is a failure of tooling health: the data pipeline is broken, so detection rules cannot fire even though they are correct. Test it by stopping a source on purpose and checking that an alert is raised, and repeat the check after every upgrade.

questions.stem: Failed-login logs contain the password the user typed. Which rule is broken?
options: Extend retention
Synchronise clocks
Add correlation IDs
Do not log secrets
questions.explanation: Logging hygiene means never writing secrets or full personal data to logs. A typed password in a failed-login record turns the log store into a credential database.

questions.stem: Which is the classic NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 phase order?
options: Govern; identify; protect; detect; respond; recover, as in the CSF 2.0 core
Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity
Detection and analysis; preparation; recovery; containment and eradication; lessons learned
Reconnaissance; weaponisation; delivery; exploitation; installation; command and control; actions on objectives
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 lists preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity. Rev. 3 treats response as part of risk management and maps to CSF 2.0.

questions.stem: A team has nightly backups but has never restored one. What is the correct assessment?
options: Backups are verified well enough by comparing the file sizes each night
Nightly backups guarantee recovery, so no further checks are needed
A backup counts only after a restore has worked, so run restore drills
Restore tests are needed only after a ransomware attack has happened
questions.explanation: A backup counts only once a restore has worked. Run restore drills, record the result and compare it with the recovery objectives (RPO and RTO).

questions.stem: Which backup property protects against ransomware that encrypts every reachable copy?
options: Compression
At least one offline or immutable copy
A second copy on the same server
A longer file-name prefix
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts every copy it can reach, so keep at least one offline or immutable copy. This is the off-site and offline part of the 3-2-1 idea.

questions.stem: What is the first step of the vulnerability management cycle in the hub?
options: Close all findings
Patch everything
Inventory assets and their owners
Scan with an exploit framework
questions.explanation: Vulnerability management starts with an inventory of assets and their owners; you cannot assess, prioritise or patch what you do not know exists.

questions.stem: What is Sigma?
options: An EDR product
A penetration-test methodology
A shared format for detection rules
A log shipping protocol
questions.explanation: Sigma is a vendor-neutral format for writing a detection rule once and converting it for many SIEMs; rules are often mapped to ATT&CK techniques. It is neither a product nor a log protocol.

questions.stem: A SOC receives thousands of alerts a day and nearly all are false positives. Which metric and action fit best?
options: Track the false-positive rate and tune the rules
Track attendance and add staff
Investigate only critical alerts indefinitely
Disable the SIEM
questions.explanation: A flood of false positives hides real incidents. Track the false-positive rate (and the alert-to-incident ratio) and tune the rules rather than ignoring alerts or only adding staff.

questions.stem: Why hold a blameless post-incident review?
options: To identify which employee was at fault and record it in their file
To find root causes and turn them into tracked fixes and detections
To satisfy a legal hold and for no other operational purpose
To avoid having to write the formal incident report afterwards
questions.explanation: A blameless review looks for root causes, for example with the 5 Whys, and turns them into tracked fixes and new detections. Blame makes people hide information.

questions.stem: Which functions does NIST CSF 2.0 define?
options: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Plan, Do, Check, Act
Prepare, Prevent, Detect, Contain, Learn
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover only
questions.explanation: NIST CSF 2.0 has six functions. Govern is the one added in version 2.0 to the original five.

questions.stem: Within what time must a personal data breach normally be notified to the regulator under the GDPR?
options: 7 days
72 hours
24 hours
30 days
questions.explanation: GDPR Article 33 requires notifying the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach.

questions.stem: Which incident-reporting steps does NIS2 use?
options: Early warning at 12 hours, notification at 48 hours and a final report after seven days
Early warning at 24 hours, notification at 72 hours and a final report after one month
One consolidated report each year, covering every incident of the previous twelve months
A single notification within 14 days of the incident, with no follow-up report
questions.explanation: NIS2 uses three steps: an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report after one month. National transposition can vary.

questions.stem: What does DORA require for designated financial entities?
options: A public bug bounty programme that runs all year round
Only quarterly vulnerability scanning, with no penetration testing
Threat-led penetration testing at least every three years
A tabletop exercise once a year and no technical testing
questions.explanation: DORA has applied since 17 January 2025. It requires threat-led penetration testing at least every three years for the financial entities that authorities designate, within a wider resilience testing programme.

questions.stem: From 11 September 2026 a manufacturer learns that a vulnerability in its product sold in the EU is being actively exploited. What is the first reporting step?
options: Notify customers only
Wait for a patch, then notify
Send the final report within 14 days of discovery
Send an early warning within 24 hours
questions.explanation: The Cyber Resilience Act sets 24 hours, 72 hours and a final report 14 days after a fix is available.

questions.stem: How do ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002 differ?
options: 27001 is a control catalogue, and 27002 is the certification scheme
They are regional versions of one standard, used in Europe and Asia
27002 replaced 27001 in 2022 and is now the only certifiable ISO standard
27001 sets certifiable ISMS requirements; 27002 is the control catalogue
questions.explanation: ISO/IEC 27001 sets the certifiable requirements for an ISMS, and ISO/IEC 27002 is the control catalogue that supports it. The control numbers were not re-checked in this hub.

questions.stem: An organisation meets every item of a compliance checklist and is still breached. Which statement explains this?
options: The auditor must have been wrong
Compliance tests are always automated
Checklists are illegal
Compliance shows conformance, not resistance
questions.explanation: Compliance shows conformance to a checklist, not resistance to an attacker. Testing only the checklist gives false assurance, so also test how the controls hold up.

questions.stem: What distinguishes mandatory from voluntary standards?
options: Mandatory ones are free to use; voluntary ones are sold by standards bodies
Mandatory ones apply nationally only; voluntary ones are always international in scope
Voluntary standards cannot be audited, so no one can certify against them
Mandatory ones stem from law or contract; voluntary ones are adopted by choice
questions.explanation: Mandatory standards come from law, regulation or contract, and voluntary ones are adopted as good practice. The choice changes how strictly you must test against them.

questions.stem: What should a risk register entry include?
options: An owner, a treatment, a target date and the residual risk
Only a severity colour, which is enough to rank all of the risks
The name of the scanner that first detected the issue
A list of the staff passwords that relate to the risk
questions.explanation: A usable risk entry names an owner, the chosen treatment, a target date and the residual risk. Test findings are risk statements, not only defects.

questions.stem: How should a security tool be selected, in ISTQB's view?
options: From documented needs and a trial, not from a vendor demo
By picking the tool that is most popular among the competitors
By choosing the cheapest licence that is available
By counting the number of features that each vendor lists
questions.explanation: ISTQB advises selecting tools from documented needs: weigh fit, result quality (false positives and negatives on your own code, in a proof of concept), open-source risks, vendor capabilities and cost.

questions.stem: An unauthenticated DAST scan finds almost nothing. What is the most likely reason?
options: It could not get past the login page; configure test accounts per role
The application is perfectly secure, so there was simply nothing to find
The scanner ran too fast for the application to respond to it
HTTPS encryption prevents scanners from sending any requests
questions.explanation: An unauthenticated DAST scan sees only the public surface, so most of the application is never exercised. Configure test accounts for each role and verify that the scanner stays logged in.

questions.stem: What distinguishes static from dynamic security tools?
options: Static tools are free, while dynamic tools always need a licence
Dynamic tools never use a network, while static tools always do
Static tools test only mobile apps; dynamic tools test only web applications
Static tools inspect without running the system; dynamic tools run it
questions.explanation: Static tools inspect code or configuration without running the system, while dynamic tools exercise the running system. ISTQB also classes tools as white-box, black-box or grey-box.

questions.stem: Which tool class finds a leaked API key in a repository's history?
options: DAST, which crawls and attacks the running web application
Fuzzing, which sends mutated inputs to a parser or service
TLS scanners, which check protocol versions and certificates
Secret scanning, for example Gitleaks or TruffleHog
questions.explanation: Secret scanning tools such as Gitleaks and TruffleHog search the whole history of a repository for keys and tokens. Run them pre-commit and as a history scan.

questions.stem: How should scanner output be treated?
options: As legal evidence once the scan has been archived
As proof of compliance with the standard being tested
As a lead to be verified manually, not as a verdict
As a final verdict that can go straight into the report
questions.explanation: Scanners produce candidates, including false positives and missed issues. Treat output as a lead, verify each finding manually, add a severity rationale, and only then report it.

questions.stem: You run Juice Shop locally and want only your own machine to reach it. Which setting achieves this?
options: Bind to 0.0.0.0
Turn off the firewall
Use host networking on a shared network
Bind the published port to 127.0.0.1
questions.explanation: Binding the published port to 127.0.0.1 keeps the deliberately vulnerable app off the network, for example docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop. Binding to 0.0.0.0 would expose it to everyone who can reach the host.

questions.stem: Why verify checksums or signatures of downloaded security tools?
options: Security tools are themselves a supply-chain target
To make the download complete faster on slow links
To unlock free licences for the paid tool editions
To avoid having to install updates for the tool later
questions.explanation: Security tools run with high privileges and are themselves a supply-chain target, so download them from official sources, verify checksums or signatures and pin versions.

questions.stem: What is a sensible first step when rolling out a SAST tool?
options: Start with a high-confidence rule subset and expand
Fail every build on any finding, whatever its severity
Run it only once, just before each major release
Enable every rule at once to maximise the coverage
questions.explanation: Turning on every rule at once buries teams in noise and they stop reading results. Start with a high-confidence rule subset, fix or triage, then expand.

rows.whatGoesWrong: Users act outside their permissions; SSRF is now part of this category
rows.testIdeas: Swap object IDs between two accounts; call admin functions as a low role; force-browse hidden URLs; point server-side fetch features at internal addresses
rows.prevention: Deny by default; enforce per object and function on the server; central access checks; allow-list outbound destinations

rows.whatGoesWrong: Default settings, open features, verbose errors, over-broad cloud permissions
rows.testIdeas: Check default accounts and consoles, directory listing, debug endpoints, security headers, storage permissions, TLS settings
rows.prevention: Hardened baselines; minimal features; automated configuration checks

rows.whatGoesWrong: Compromised or vulnerable dependencies, build systems and distribution paths
rows.testIdeas: Inventory dependencies and build steps; check pinning, signatures and provenance; look for dependency-confusion exposure
rows.prevention: SBOM; pinned and verified dependencies; hardened CI/CD; signed artifacts; update policy

rows.whatGoesWrong: Missing or weak protection of data in transit and at rest
rows.testIdeas: Inspect protocols and ciphers; look for clear-text data, weak password hashing, hard-coded keys, predictable tokens
rows.prevention: TLS everywhere; strong modern algorithms; key management; Argon2id for passwords

rows.whatGoesWrong: Untrusted input is interpreted as code or commands (SQL, OS, template, script in pages)
rows.testIdeas: Partition inputs and try boundary and special-character values; watch for errors, changed behaviour and unescaped output; review how queries and output are built
rows.prevention: Parameterised queries; context-aware output encoding; validation as defence in depth; least-privilege database accounts

rows.whatGoesWrong: Missing or ineffective controls at design level; abusable business logic
rows.testIdeas: Review the threat model; test workflow abuse such as skipped steps, replay, quantity and price manipulation, races
rows.prevention: Threat modelling; secure design patterns; abuse-case requirements; limits on sensitive flows

rows.whatGoesWrong: Weak login, recovery or session handling
rows.testIdeas: Test lockout and rate limits, password policy, MFA enforcement, reset tokens, session fixation and logout
rows.prevention: MFA; breached-password checks; secure session management; uniform error messages

rows.whatGoesWrong: Code or data trusted without integrity checks; unsafe deserialization
rows.testIdeas: Review update and plugin mechanisms; check signature verification; test deserialization points and unsigned client data
rows.prevention: Signed code and data; integrity checks on updates and pipelines; avoid deserializing untrusted data

rows.whatGoesWrong: Attacks leave no usable trace and trigger no alert
rows.testIdeas: Cause login failures, access violations and admin actions; verify they are logged, correlated and alerted; check logs for secrets
rows.prevention: Log security events with context; protect log integrity; alert on defined conditions; test the alerts

rows.whatGoesWrong: Poor error handling, logic errors, failing open
rows.testIdeas: Force timeouts, malformed input and dependency failures; confirm the system fails closed without leaking details
rows.prevention: Central error handling; fail closed; resource limits; tests for failure paths

rows.name: Broken Object Level Authorization

rows.testIdeas: With two accounts, request each object type, including list, search, export and batch endpoints, using the other account's IDs; hard-to-guess IDs are not a control

rows.name: Broken Authentication
rows.whatGoesWrong: Weak token handling, no limits on login or reset, loose token validation
rows.testIdeas: Check token expiry, reuse after logout, signature and claim validation, reset-flow tokens, throttling of credential guessing
rows.prevention: Standard authentication libraries; short-lived tokens; rate limits; strict validation of signature, issuer, audience and expiry

rows.name: Broken Object Property Level Authorization

rows.testIdeas: Compare response fields across roles; add unexpected properties such as role or price to write requests and check they are ignored or rejected

rows.name: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
rows.whatGoesWrong: No limits on rate, size, pagination or cost
rows.testIdeas: Within agreed limits, test large page sizes, deep nesting, big payloads, batch sizes and repeated costly operations
rows.prevention: Quotas, rate limits, payload and time limits, spend caps for paid back-end calls

rows.name: Broken Function Level Authorization
rows.whatGoesWrong: Ordinary users reach administrative functions by changing the method or path
rows.testIdeas: Call admin endpoints and write methods as a low role; try methods the documentation does not list
rows.prevention: Deny by default; role checks per function; separate administrative routes

rows.name: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
rows.whatGoesWrong: Automation abuses a legitimate flow at scale, such as vouchers, bookings or sign-ups
rows.testIdeas: Script repeated runs of the flow; check per-user and per-device limits and step-up checks
rows.prevention: Identify sensitive flows; limit and monitor them; add friction where abuse pays

rows.name: Server Side Request Forgery
rows.whatGoesWrong: The API fetches a URL the caller controls
rows.testIdeas: In a lab, give webhook, import and image-fetch parameters internal and loopback targets and see whether they are fetched

rows.name: Security Misconfiguration

rows.testIdeas: Review CORS rules, headers, error bodies, debug modes and enabled methods
rows.prevention: Repeatable hardened configuration; automated checks in CI

rows.name: Improper Inventory Management

rows.testIdeas: Look for older versions and non-production hosts; compare real traffic with the OpenAPI document
rows.prevention: Maintain an inventory; retire old versions; document every endpoint

rows.name: Unsafe Consumption of APIs

rows.prevention: Treat upstream data as untrusted; validate, set timeouts, verify TLS

rows.testIdea: Hide instructions in documents, web pages, emails and tool output the system ingests, and check whether it obeys them against policy; repeat across languages and multi-turn chats
rows.control: Separate privileges; treat model output as untrusted; require human approval for high-impact actions

rows.testIdea: Probe for other users' or tenants' data, secrets in context and memorised data; check retrieval permissions
rows.control: Data minimisation; per-user retrieval authorization; output filtering

rows.testIdea: Inventory models, datasets, plugins and libraries; verify provenance and file formats
rows.control: Vetted sources; signed models; AI bill of materials

rows.testIdea: Review how training, fine-tuning and embedding data are collected and approved; run trigger and drift evaluations
rows.control: Data validation and versioning; access control; red-team evaluations

rows.testIdea: Make the model emit markup or command-like strings and see whether downstream code interprets them
rows.control: Encode and validate output like any untrusted input

rows.testIdea: List the tools and permissions; try to make the agent act beyond the caller's own rights
rows.control: Least privilege; narrow tools; user-scoped credentials; human in the loop

rows.testIdea: Try to extract hidden instructions; look for credentials or internal rules inside them
rows.control: No secrets in prompts; enforce rules outside the prompt

rows.testIdea: Test cross-tenant retrieval, injected documents and leakage from embeddings
rows.control: Access control on vector stores; ingestion checks; tenant isolation

rows.testIdea: Run grounded-answer and citation checks on domain question sets
rows.control: Retrieval grounding; human review; interfaces that signal uncertainty

rows.testIdea: Test long inputs, runaway agent loops, rate limits and cost caps

rows.howItWorks: A deceptive message pushes a click or a credential entry
rows.controls: Mail filtering, phishing-resistant MFA, a report button, training
rows.ethicalTest: Authorised simulations measuring click, submit and report rates; collect no real passwords unless agreed

rows.howItWorks: A caller talks staff into a reset or disclosure
rows.ethicalTest: Scripted pretext calls agreed with management

rows.howItWorks: Text messages carry lures and links
A found USB stick or QR code tempts use
rows.ethicalTest: Controlled drops with a harmless marker

rows.howItWorks: Following an authorised person through a door
rows.controls: Badge discipline, mantraps, a culture of challenge
rows.ethicalTest: Physical tests with a signed authorisation letter carried at all times

rows.howItWorks: An impersonated executive or supplier asks for a payment or data
Repeated push prompts until someone approves
rows.controls: Number matching, rate limits, phishing-resistant MFA
rows.ethicalTest: Test the configuration, not the staff

rows.howItWorks: Synthetic media impersonates a trusted person

rows.what: Endpoint, identity, network, cloud control-plane, application and email logs
rows.howToTest: Perform known actions (failed logins, privilege change, admin action, sensitive data read) and confirm each leaves a record with actor, time, target and result

rows.what: Central, time-synchronised, tamper-resistant storage with a retention policy
rows.howToTest: Check clock sync and UTC timestamps; try to alter or delete logs with a normal and an admin account; confirm retention matches policy

rows.what: SIEM or EDR logic, often written in a shared format such as Sigma and mapped to ATT&CK techniques
rows.howToTest: Replay harmless simulations of a technique in a lab (for example Atomic Red Team) and check the rule fires; track which techniques have no rule
Measure time from event to alert to human action; test that alerts reach someone awake
Alert when a source goes silent; test after upgrades

rows.name: NIST CSF 2.0
rows.what: Voluntary framework published in February 2024 with six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
rows.hooks: Structure a programme and its test outcomes; profiles describe current and target state

rows.name: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and 27002:2022
rows.what: Certifiable ISMS requirements and a control catalogue of 93 controls
rows.hooks: Control 8.29 (security testing in development and acceptance) and 8.8 (technical vulnerabilities); internal audit evidence. Control numbers not re-checked

rows.name: CIS Controls v8.1
rows.hooks: A practical baseline; penetration testing and vulnerability management are controls in their own right

rows.name: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
rows.what: Catalogue of security and privacy controls
rows.hooks: Penetration testing (CA-8), vulnerability scanning (RA-5), developer testing (SA-11). Identifiers not re-checked

rows.name: PCI DSS v4.0.1
rows.hooks: Requirement 11: regular scans, penetration tests at least annually and after significant change, segmentation tests. Not re-checked

rows.name: SOC 2
rows.what: AICPA attestation against the trust services criteria
rows.hooks: Evidence of vulnerability management, change control and testing

rows.name: GDPR
rows.hooks: Article 32 expects security appropriate to the risk, including regular testing of its effectiveness; Article 33 sets a 72-hour breach notification to the regulator

rows.name: NIS2 (Directive 2022/2555)
rows.what: EU rules for essential and important entities
rows.hooks: Risk-management measures include assessing their own effectiveness; incident reports follow 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month steps. National transposition varies, so check local law

rows.name: DORA (Regulation 2022/2554)
rows.what: EU digital operational resilience for financial entities, applying from 17 January 2025
rows.hooks: A resilience testing programme, with threat-led penetration testing for designated entities at least every three years

rows.name: EU Cyber Resilience Act
rows.what: Cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements
rows.hooks: From 11 September 2026 manufacturers report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents: early warning in 24 hours, notification in 72 hours, final report 14 days after a fix is available (or one month for severe incidents), through a single reporting platform. Main obligations apply from December 2027 (from memory)
